title: Non-Equilibrium Dynamics Neural Networks (NBDNN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Non-Equilibrium Dynamics Neural Networks (NBDNN), a novel approach to neural network design that leverages the principles of non-equilibrium dynamics. The core claim is that neural networks can achieve more sophisticated pattern recognition and generation by mimicking the behavior of non-equilibrium systems. This is achieved through a network architecture based on neural networks incorporating equations derived from non-equilibrium dynamics. The mechanism relies on simulating the dynamical evolution of systems in non-equilibrium states, employing self-organized criticality to drive pattern generation. We demonstrate that this approach overcomes limitations inherent in traditional neural networks by exploiting the inherent complexity arising from systems operating far from equilibrium. The proposed NBDNN architecture offers a pathway to generating novel and complex patterns, potentially applicable in diverse fields such as image generation, time series analysis, and complex system modeling. The network is trained using backpropagation, adapting the weights to minimize the difference between the simulated dynamics and the target patterns. Further research will focus on optimizing the network architecture and exploring the influence of different non-equilibrium dynamics models.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Modeling Complex Systems with Time-Varying Dependencies
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) for modeling complex systems exhibiting time-varying dependencies. Traditional DBNs often struggle with accurately representing evolving relationships between variables over time, leading to limitations in their predictive capabilities. This work proposes an extension to the standard DBN framework incorporating adaptive learning mechanisms. These mechanisms enable the network to dynamically adjust its structure and parameters in response to observed changes in the system dynamics. The core claim is that this adaptive approach significantly improves the ability of DBNs to model intricate dependencies and provides a more flexible and robust solution compared to static DBN models. Specifically, we explore methods for updating the network's conditional dependencies and parameter estimates based on temporal data streams. The resulting model demonstrates superior performance in scenarios where the underlying system is non-stationary. The research contributes a novel approach to DBN modeling, offering a pathway for tackling complex, real-world systems with evolving characteristics.

title: Non-Euclidean Vector Field Modeling with Adaptive Complexity
abstract: This paper presents a novel method for modeling vector fields in non-Euclidean space, leveraging a self-adjusting complexity metric. Traditional methods struggle with the inherent complexity of these fields, often requiring extensive parameter tuning and limited predictive power. Our approach introduces a "complexity gradient" that dynamically adjusts the mathematical complexity of the vector field, enabling the model to capture a wider range of behavior and improving predictive accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of simulations and analysis, showcasing its ability to model complex and varied field patterns with significantly reduced parameterization. The core mechanism focuses on creating a self-regulating system that adapts to the data's inherent complexity, offering a robust and adaptable solution for a wide range of applications.

title: AI-Enhanced Personalized Learning Systems in Education
abstract: In this paper we propose an AI-based personalized learning system which is capable of addressing the shortcomings in adaptive, extendible and interpretable functionality of current systems. The model combines reinforcement learning, federated learning, and explainable AI to adapt the educational material in real time according to learner behavior and context. It gives both privacy-preserving student profiling and pedagogically sound feedback, as opposed to its classical counterparts. Experimental results show that the learning efficiency, engagement and performance are enhanced in different environments. The modular nature of the system enables scaling with institutionally owned resources and ensures adherence to ethical and privacy regulations.

title: The DescryptTool: agentic LLM-based workbench for decipherment of historical ciphers
abstract: The DescryptTool is an agentic research workbench developed within the DESCRYPT project to support the cryptanalysis of historical ciphers. Its contribution is not a new cipher-solving algorithm alone, but a controlled architecture in which a large language model (LLM) can use existing cryptanalytic modules through explicit, auditable tool calls. The system separates two roles: (i) the Observer, a read-only assistant that explains the current analytical state and proposes next steps, and (ii) the Orchestrator, an execution mode that can plan, configure, run, and document complete analysis workflows subject to user-controlled permissions. DescryptTool combines a project-based PyQt workbench, local solvers for simple substitution, Vigenère, and homophonic substitution, reusable text workflows, local logging, and persistent SQLite-based memory. This article presents the system architecture, the tool-control model, solver capabilities and limitations, and an evaluation on synthetic and historical ciphertexts. The results show that agentic workflow control can make established cryptanalytic practice more transparent, teachable, and reproducible, while also exposing clear limits: stochastic solvers are not bit-reproducible without recorded random seeds, LLM recommendations may be wrong, and historical systems with nomenclature elements still require expert validation.

title: CANAL: Channel-Aware Noise Allocation for Differentially Private Feature Distillation in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical image segmentation needs diverse training data, but hospitals hold complementary scans they cannot share for privacy and regulatory reasons. Knowledge distillation can bridge this gap by exporting learned feature representations instead of images, but those representations still encode patient-specific anatomy and remain vulnerable to membership-inference and feature-inversion attacks. Adding calibrated Gaussian noise restores a differential-privacy guarantee, yet three issues have been overlooked. First, prior DP feature-distillation pipelines re-sample noise at every student iteration, so each patient image is released many times and the privacy cost composes over those releases, growing by orders of magnitude. We present a sample-once-per-image release, realized by a single precomputation pass, under which each patient contributes one release. Second, uniform noise is wasteful because channels differ in task importance. Using task-gradient energy as the importance measure, we derive CANAL, a closed-form water-filling allocation that gives important channels proportionally less noise, and prove it strictly minimizes importance-weighted distortion at a fixed budget. Third, the clipping caps and importance scores that drive the allocation are themselves data-dependent, so releasing them in the clear silently breaks the guarantee. We give a DP-honest budget split that charges each to the privacy budget, so the reported epsilon is the true epsilon. Across three medical segmentation benchmarks spanning dermoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound, CANAL retains more task-relevant signal than uniform noise at the same privacy budget.

title: Modus Tollens and Counterfactuals and Counterfactual Reasoning Based on Three Types of Negation
abstract: Modus Tollens (MT) is a classical logical inference rule, while counterfactuals are hypothetical statements that are contrary to facts, and counterfactual reasoning is a process of reasoning based on counterfactuals. Negation is an indispensable core concept in them. In this paper, based on the logical systems LCOI&PLCOI with contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation, we propose three variants of Modus Tollens corresponding to distinct negation types, namely MTC: Modus Tollens based on contradictory negation, MTO: Modus Tollens based on opposite negation, and MTI: Modus Tollens based on intermediary negation. We define the implications within MTC, MTO and MTI, provide the truth value algorithms of MTC, MTO and MTI, and discuss the reducibility of these algorithms. To incorporate these three types of negation into counterfactuals and counterfactual reasoning, we differentiate counterfactuals into two types based on whether they possess logical negation, thereby proposing three counterfactuals and counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations. In this paper, we further argue that the three counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations have the same inference form as MTC, MTO and MTI, respectively. In other words, they share the same inference structure. As a result, the truth value algorithms for MTC, MTO and MTI can be as the truth value algorithms for the three counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations. The algorithms indicates that if the first premise of the reasoning is true, the truth values of the reasoning conclusions are identical to the truth values of the three negative premises in the reasoning premises, respectively. This reflects the consistency and accuracy of the truth value algorithms.

title: CSN Quantum Computing Processes in the Human Brain
abstract: CSN stands for Catalin Silviu Nutu, and it is the acronym for the name of the author who has developed the theory related to the CSN Algorithm, such as presented in his previous work published so far. Current conventional and classical AI models today, mainly based on supervised and unsupervised learning, have almost reached their limits, and they are completely insufficient and totally inadequate to simulate and to model highly sophisticated and complicated brain processes involved in highly creative and extremely innovative brain processes. Based on the theory introduced, developed and presented by the author related to the CSN Algorithm and by introducing a new type of special matrix named CSN Matrix of Activations, this paper generates a quantum computing model named CSN Quantum Computing brain model. This paper expands on the latest work of the author presented in his last papers on this topic, namely “Decryption of Evolutionary Fractals by means of Procedural Randomness generated with an Intelligence Model based on the CSN Algorithm”, presented at the International Conference XR Salento 2025 in Otranto, Italy, and a subsequent paper entitled “Enhanced Intelligence Models based on the CSN Algorithm”, also published in 2025, in the International Journal of Computational Engineering Research (IJCER)

title: Executable Matrix-Product Unitaries: A Geometric Operator Framework for Quantum Circuits
abstract: Quantum circuit theory has long treated Matrix‑Product Unitaries (MPUs) as elegant but unreachable objects—beautiful on paper, impossible to extract, and as far as we know never once executed on real hardware. This work breaks that barrier. We introduce the first geometric MPU extraction pipeline capable of reconstructing full multi‑qubit unitaries with machine‑precision fidelity, validating them across uniform CZ layers, bidirectional sweeps, non‑uniform constructions, QFT‑derived operators, high‑bond entangling layers, and multi‑layer MPU compositions. Every MPU class tested—without exception—compiles cleanly through Qiskit into hardware‑native CX+U3 circuits, producing thousands‑gate decompositions that match the original MPU operators with Frobenius error near 10^{-11} and fidelity 1.0. For the first time, MPUs move from abstract tensor‑network theory into executable quantum computation. This establishes a practical bridge between MPU mathematics and real quantum devices, opening a new path for hardware‑compatible tensor‑network operators, circuit compression, and quantum algorithm design.

title: Dynamic Probability Graphs: Modeling and Optimization of Complex Systems
abstract: Dynamic Probability Graphs (DPGs) represent a novel approach to modeling complex systems by dynamically updating graph structures based on real-time environmental changes. This paper introduces a method employing reinforcement learning and evolutionary algorithms to optimize the graph structure, ensuring model predictability and accurate system behavior prediction. The core mechanism focuses on a continuous adjustment process, dynamically responding to evolving conditions. Traditional approaches often suffer from static models, failing to capture the dynamic nature of real-world systems. This research addresses this limitation by creating a flexible and adaptive representation, offering improved predictive capabilities and optimization potential.

title: Adaptive Dynamic Probability Model
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for probabilistic modeling, termed the Adaptive Dynamic Probability Model (ADPM), that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on data. The core innovation lies in a self-adaptive parameter adjustment mechanism, enabling the model to continuously optimize its predictive accuracy. This approach contrasts with static probabilistic models, offering increased efficiency and adaptability. We detail the framework's architecture, explain the self-adjustment process, and demonstrate its efficacy through illustrative examples, highlighting its potential for improved predictive performance across various applications.

title: Dynamic Geometric Transformations and Quantum Spin Effects
abstract: This paper investigates the influence of dynamic geometric transformations on quantum spin effects, proposing a novel quantum spin computation framework leveraging the unique quantum properties of spin. We aim to predict and control the evolution of dynamic geometric transformations, ultimately enabling high-precision quantum calculations. The core mechanism centers around utilizing spin's quantum nature to guide and manipulate geometric configurations, providing a fundamentally new approach to quantum computation. This work addresses the limitations of existing static models by introducing a dynamic, self-correcting framework optimized for spin-based calculations. The research highlights the potential of this approach to significantly advance the field of quantum information processing.

title: Quantum Error Correction: Adaptive Synchronization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a critical component of quantum computation, enabling the reliable manipulation of quantum states. Current synchronization algorithms, however, often struggle to maintain the required accuracy and speed, particularly in the face of environmental noise. This paper introduces a novel adaptive synchronization algorithm based on quantum error correction principles. The core mechanism leverages the dynamic adjustment of quantum states during the error correction process to achieve higher precision and faster computation, effectively mitigating the impact of noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations, showcasing its potential to significantly improve the performance of quantum processors. Keywords: Quantum Error Correction, Adaptive Synchronization, Quantum State Synchronization, Quantum Computation, Noise Mitigation.

title: Quantum-Guided Constraint Optimization (QGCO)
abstract: Quantum-Guided Constraint Optimization (QGCO) presents a novel approach to solving complex optimization problems by integrating quantum annealing with constraint optimization techniques. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum annealing to accelerate the search process while simultaneously enforcing constraints, resulting in enhanced solution quality. We delve into the theoretical framework, algorithmic implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating the efficacy of this method. The core claim focuses on the synergistic combination of quantum annealing and constraint optimization to achieve a significant improvement in optimization speed and solution quality compared to traditional methods. This research addresses limitations of existing techniques by providing a robust and efficient framework for tackling challenging optimization problems across diverse domains.

title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning via Contrastive Relational Embedding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-supervised representation learning approach for graph data, termed Contrastive Relational Embedding. The core challenge in leveraging graphs for machine learning lies in effectively capturing the intricate relationships between nodes. Existing self-supervised methods often fall short in this regard, primarily focusing on unsupervised node embeddings without explicitly considering the relational context. Our method addresses this limitation by training a neural network to learn embeddings that reflect the underlying graph structure through a contrastive learning framework. Specifically, we define relationships as 'neighbor' and 'connected-to' and use a contrastive loss to pull together embeddings of nodes that share these relations, while pushing apart the embeddings of nodes with different relations. This approach allows the model to learn rich, graph-aware representations without relying on manual annotations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline, highlighting its potential for improved performance in downstream graph-related tasks.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN BREAST CANCER SCREENING: A REVIEW
authors: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN BREAST CANCER SCREENING: A REVIEW
abstract: Abstract Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer among women worldwide, and early detection through screening remains essential for reducing mortality. Mammography is the standard screening modality; however, its diagnostic performance may be affected by false positive results, false-negative findings, reduced sensitivity in dense breast tissue, and variability in image interpretation. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning and deep learning, have enhanced breast cancer screening by improving lesion detection, image classification, risk prediction, and workflow efficiency. AI has been successfully applied to mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging, demonstrating promising improvements in diagnostic accuracy and screening performance. Despite these advances, challenges such as limited dataset diversity, algorithm bias, lack of interpretability, regulatory concerns, data privacy, and integration into clinical practice remain barriers to widespread implementation. Ongoing research focusing on robust validation, ethical AI development, and multidisciplinary collaboration is expected to facilitate the safe and effective adoption of AI in breast cancer screening. This review summarizes current applications of AI in breast cancer screening, highlights its clinical benefits and limitations, and discusses future perspectives for integrating AI into evidence-based and personalized breast cancer screening programs.

abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum entanglement weaving algorithm that dynamically constructs and adjusts quantum entanglement networks for improved quantum communication and quantum computation. Traditional entanglement weaving methods are often static, limiting efficiency. Our algorithm leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to adjust the size and structure of entangled networks in response to specific requirements, offering a significant advancement over existing approaches. We explore the core mechanism of this dynamic adjustment through a novel control strategy. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach to enhance quantum communication and quantum computation through adaptive network design.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: Distributed Coprocessor
abstract: This paper proposes a novel architecture for distributed coprocessor networks leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to utilize entangled nodes for ultra-fast, secure data transmission and computation, overcoming the limitations of traditional distributed computing systems. We detail a mechanism for constructing a network of entangled nodes, employing entanglement-based measurements and manipulations to facilitate data exchange and computation. The use of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols ensures the security of the communication channel. This approach offers a significant advancement over conventional methods, providing enhanced bandwidth, improved security, and the potential for distributed computing capabilities across extended distances. The theoretical framework and underlying principles are presented, outlining a pathway toward realizing a quantum-enhanced distributed coprocessor network.

title: Adaptive Topological Transformation Algorithm for Quantum Computing (ATTC)
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Topological Transformation Algorithm (ATTC) for quantum computing, designed to dynamically manipulate quantum states. Traditional quantum computation often relies on static state representations, limiting the ability to precisely simulate quantum system behavior. The ATTC leverages topological transformations, a powerful tool in quantum geometry, to optimize quantum states for enhanced efficiency and robustness. This algorithm dynamically adjusts the quantum state structure during a transformation process, resulting in improved performance metrics. The core mechanism focuses on optimizing the quantum state's geometry through a series of carefully designed topological operations. This innovation promises to significantly improve the capabilities of quantum algorithms, particularly in areas requiring precise modeling and dynamic adaptation. We present a comprehensive analysis of the ATTC's design and performance, demonstrating its potential to advance quantum computing paradigms.

abstract: Abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computation to revolutionize the field of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). The core mechanism relies on representing the CSP graph as a quantum state and employing superposition to efficiently explore multiple solution paths concurrently. This approach promises significant speedups compared to classical approaches, particularly for large and complex CSPs. The paper details the algorithm's design, potential benefits, and preliminary results demonstrating improved performance.

title: Support Vector Machines for Classification, Regression, and Outlier Detection: A Tutorial
abstract: Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a fundamental machine learning method based on the principle of maximum-margin learning. This chapter develops SVM from its geometric intuition to its optimization formulation and extensions. We first contrast SVM with the Perceptron and motivate the use of the maximum-margin decision boundary. We then derive hard-margin SVM, including the primal and dual optimization problems, the role of Lagrange multipliers, the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions, and the interpretation of support vectors. Soft-margin SVM is subsequently introduced to handle approximately linearly separable data through slack variables and regularization. For nonlinear classification, kernelization and the kernel trick are presented, leading to kernel SVM in which inner products are replaced by kernel evaluations in a possibly high-dimensional feature space. The chapter then extends the support-vector framework beyond classification to Support Vector Regression (SVR), where an $\varepsilon$-insensitive tube is used for regression, and to one-class SVM, where a separating boundary is learned for novelty and outlier detection. Throughout the chapter, emphasis is placed on the connections between geometry, convex optimization, duality, KKT conditions, sparsity, and the role of support vectors across the different formulations.

title: Natural Language Processing for Human–Computer Interaction
abstract: In this work we propose an advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework for HCI that handles some of the important challenges such as multilingualism, emotional intelligence, context preservation, and explainability. Utilising transformer-based models, memory-augmented networks, and privacy-preserving learning, the system guarantees robust, adaptive and empathetic interaction in any domain. It allows real-time conversation, cross-domain understanding, and dynamic behavior modeling, without compromising data privacy. The proposed framework also focuses on the scalability, standard evaluation protocols, and ethical compliance for commercialization, which drive it to be a versatile, secure, and unified platform that enable large-scale deployment in next-genre HCI systems.

title: Scaling Multi-Agent Systems with Prospect-State Propagation
abstract: Current LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) periodically compress intermediate states to reduce inference-time token consumption, thereby attempting to incorporate more agents. However, naive scaling strategies face challenges. For example, in economic simulations, large-scale MAS typically discard semantically rich economic states, i.e., agent behavioral trajectories, which are key drivers of macroeconomic fluctuations. In this paper, we reveal a phenomenon in which agent heterogeneity gradually decreases during simulation, and propose Prospect-State Propagation for Multi-Agent Systems (PspMAS). Inspired by prospect theory, PspMAS decouples each agent's micro state into a compact Prospect State and an expressive Semantic State. The former records psychological traces through a lightweight, parallelizable propagator and continuously injects heterogeneity into the system. The latter leverages the strong perception, reasoning, planning, and decision-making abilities of LLMs. These two components work complementarily, providing a scalable LLM-based multi-agent simulation solution.

title: Computing with logarithmicstate and history
abstract: A computation can return to its original state while retaining a nonzero history of interaction. We presentthe application of exact logarithmic state/history in the Substrate Ledger Computer, implemented in SLC-GEN2-R4. Positive source-action ratios become additive coordinates, while their ordered incrementsretain cumulative rise, fall, variation and maximum excursion. These readouts distinguish an unchangedendpoint from an executed loop and recover a historical contact barrier from its logarithmic maximumand original action. An exact composition law joins history segments without changing their referenceor losing maximizing states. The same runtime represents uncertainty over complete linked histories anduses rationally weighted formal logarithms to select native probes and report resolution for a specifiedhistorical target. A four-history receiver example separates equal quantities of source information withdifferent barrier content. Adaptive two-observation policies then resolve a target with an expected 1.5readings while retaining unresolved histories, and a separate lookahead example gains information onlyafter a second interaction. Source-defined scale-and-turn coordinates, quarter-turn golden scheduling,construction-boundary information and signed contribution arithmetic share these contracts. Installedapplications connect the representation to isotope assemblies, exact frustrated-spin spectra and signedMöbius-moment calculations. The resulting method makes logarithmic history an executable object: itcan be queried, composed, used to choose an observation and continued from a complete checkpoint.Keywords: logarithmic computation; executable history; exact arithmetic; conditional reconstruction;adaptive observation; Substrate Ledger Computer

abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol designed specifically for scalable photonic networks. The protocol leverages the inherent advantages of a multi-hop, all-topological architecture to overcome the limitations of traditional QKD systems regarding key transmission distance and rate. We propose a scheme utilizing quantum entanglement and state transformations within the network to facilitate distributed key generation and secure key distribution. The core innovation lies in the network topology itself, which allows for robust error correction and eavesdropping detection, ultimately leading to a highly secure and high-throughput quantum communication system. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the protocol's resilience to various attack scenarios and highlights its potential for practical implementation in large-scale quantum networks.

title: The Geometry of Causality: Hierarchical Causality Networks and Predictive Geometry
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of geometry and causality, proposing a novel hierarchical causality network framework. We investigate how the structure of a network – defined by its connectivity and topology – directly influences the flow of causal influence, offering a new perspective on understanding and modeling causal relationships. The core claim is that causality is fundamentally geometric, and that the representation of a causal network via a geometric structure allows for predictive capabilities. This work utilizes a hierarchical network model to demonstrate the potential for this geometric approach to yield enhanced predictive accuracy. The analysis will delve into the mathematical foundations of this framework, focusing on network topology and flow dynamics. We will explore how the geometry inherent in the network structure enables a deeper understanding of causality than traditional, purely statistical approaches.

title: A Hybrid Approach: Combining Differentiable Simulation Engines with Reinforcement Learning Control
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to control and optimization of complex physical systems by integrating differentiable simulation engines with reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional control methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and nonlinearity of many physical systems, requiring extensive tuning and potentially failing to generalize well. Our methodology leverages the ability to represent physical systems as a set of differential equations, allowing for continuous, differentiable simulation. This simulation environment then serves as the basis for training an RL agent, which learns an optimal control policy through trial and error. The key innovation lies in the seamless coupling of these two techniques – the deterministic, accurate simulation providing the feedback signal for the RL agent, and the RL agent dynamically adjusting the simulation parameters to improve learning efficiency and robustness. We detail the architecture of this hybrid system, focusing on the mathematical formulation and implementation considerations. This approach offers the potential for achieving real-time control and optimization of systems that are intractable for conventional control methods. ---

title: Quantum Entanglement Computation via Algebraic Vector Representation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a unique challenge to computational efficiency. Traditional methods often struggle to efficiently handle the intricate calculations involved in quantum systems. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing algebraic vector representation to transform entanglement calculations into a set of algebraic operations, aiming to dramatically improve computational speed and provide deeper insights into the fundamental nature of quantum entanglement. We establish a new method for representing entangled states as algebraic vectors, leveraging the geometric properties of string theory to achieve this transformation. The core mechanism involves the development of a specialized algebraic vector representation that allows for efficient computation through a sequence of transformations, ultimately revealing the underlying mathematical structure of entangled states. This research explores the potential for quantum entanglement computation to be revolutionized by this algorithmic shift.

title: Quantum Bayesian Network for Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Quantum Bayesian Network (QBN) architecture specifically designed for Constraint Satisfaction problems (CSPs). We propose a QBN leveraging quantum annealing or variational quantum algorithms to efficiently explore solution spaces, enabling the handling of highly complex, multi-variable CSPs. The core mechanism involves dynamically updating constraint relationships through quantum superposition, offering a potential paradigm shift in solving these challenging problems. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a case study focusing on a simplified CSP, highlighting its ability to outperform traditional methods in terms of solution finding time and complexity. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions of this research.

title: Distributed Differential Privacy via Federated Learning with Byzantine Resilience
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without direct data sharing, thereby preserving data privacy. However, existing FL frameworks are susceptible to Byzantine attacks, where malicious participants intentionally send false information to disrupt the learning process and compromise the privacy guarantees provided by differential privacy (DP). This paper proposes a novel distributed differential privacy protocol for FL that incorporates Byzantine resilience. Our approach leverages verifiable distributed computation to detect and mitigate the influence of Byzantine participants, ensuring both privacy and robustness against malicious behavior. The core claim of this work is that FL with DP is inherently vulnerable to Byzantine attacks. The primary mechanism involves designing a federated learning protocol that actively identifies and downweights contributions from potentially malicious participants. We achieve this through a combination of outlier detection techniques and verifiable computation, guaranteeing a robust and differentially private learning outcome. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of our protocol in maintaining differential privacy while mitigating the impact of Byzantine adversaries. We provide a detailed mathematical formulation of the protocol and its privacy guarantees, focusing on the key parameters and their impact on the overall privacy budget. Finally, we outline the potential implications and future research directions for this work.

title: Consistency Is Not Correctness: What Internal Contradiction Detection Certifies, Why the Entailment Is Disjunctive, and Which Decisions It Leaves Unlicensed
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Contradiction detection occupies an unusual position among proposals for making a language model check itself. Comparing two of a model's own outputs appears to need no external oracle, which makes it look like the one exception to the observation that working hallucination detectors sit outside the model. This paper argues that the appearance is produced by running two different inferences under one word. Inconsistency supports a deductive inference: if two outputs contradict each other, at least one of them is false, and this follows from logic alone without any appeal to the world. Consistency supports only an inductive one: agreement is evidence of correctness to the extent that the model's errors are unstable under whatever perturbation produced the second output, an assumption that the sampling-based detectors state explicitly and that the strongest published instance of the family declines to extend to systematic error. The two inferences have opposite properties. The deductive one is sound and disjunctive, identifying that something is wrong without identifying which output is wrong, and so licenses withholding but not repair. The inductive one names a specific output to accept, and fails in the cases that matter most, because an error shared by both compared outputs survives the comparison intact. The paper traces the consequences: that breaking the disjunction requires an adjudicator whose errors are not those of the generator, that every published route to one is external in the relevant sense even when it runs on the same weights, and that a consistency rate is a measurement of distributional stability under a named perturbation rather than a reliability figure. Making consistency an optimization target inverts its diagnostic value, which two recent results on label-free training report directly. What is not known is stated flatly, and six measurements are specified.

title: Early Detection of Digital Transaction Fraud in Banking Systems Using the Random Forest Algorithm
abstract: This research aims to develop methods for preventing and detecting cyberattacks in banking systems by leveraging machine learning techniques.[1] Cybersecurity threats are becoming increasingly complex and pose significant risks to banking institutions and their customers through various attack types including fraud, intrusion, and malware.[2][3], [4]The data science approach utilizing machine learning enables automatic and real-time identification of anomalous patterns in transactional and security log data.[2], [5] This study utilizes transaction datasets and security logs as primary data sources. Random Forest and XGBoost models were selected due to their capability to handle high-dimensional data and class imbalance. Model evaluation was conducted using accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC metrics. The prototype implementation includes a visualization dashboard to assist end-users.[6], [7] Random Forest and XGBoost models are selected due to their capability to handle high-dimensional data and class imbalance.[8], [9] Systematic preprocessing and feature engineering steps will address missing values, normalization, and categorical encoding.[10], [11] Moreover, model evaluation will be conducted using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC to ensure optimal performance.[12] The prototype system implementation includes a visualization dashboard and automatic prediction features for end-users.[13] The expected outcomes of this research are improved early detection and prevention of cyber threats in the banking sector, contributing to the advancement of AI-based security systems in Indonesia.[14] Experimental results demonstrate that tree-based ensemble learning models significantly outperform SVM in handling extreme class imbalance. XGBoost achieved the best performance with an ROC-AUC score of 0.995, followed by Random Forest at 0.992, whereas SVM achieved only 0.935. Model transparency analysis using SHAP confirmed that transaction frequency and spikes in transaction amounts were the most critical predictors for identifying fraud. Overall, this research concludes that integrating XGBoost with the SHAP approach yields a fraud detection system that offers not only high accuracy but also clear interpretability to support decision-making in the digital banking sector.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Optimization Problems in Logistics
abstract: In this paper, we investigate a quantum approach to solve hard optimization problems of logistics, such as vehicle routing, warehouse scheduling, supply chain planning, etc. Employing quantum computation models, viz., Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) as well as hybrid quantum-classical computing framework, the proposed technique overcomes problems of scalability, constraint handling, and performance issues of previous work. The research demonstrates benchmarking on benchmarks, on logistics datasets, and across quantum platforms. We establish that the solution quality and the convergence efficiency were improved by considering the quantum annealing effect, showing that quantum computing is a revolutionary playing card in optimization for logistics.

title: Digital Image Processing
abstract: Integrate machine learning and AI-based approaches into practical image processing with Python Engineers and researchers implementing image processing systems need methods that bridge classical techniques with modern machine learning approaches. This book delivers both traditional and modern AI-based methods and algorithms in image enhancement, restoration, segmentation, compression, and analysis. Written by an educator and researcher with more than 40 years’ experience in signal/image processing and machine learning, this reference provides theoretical and practical tools using the Python platform for a wide range of applications. The book consists of twenty chapters covering fundamental and advanced topics including two-dimensional image modeling, wavelet transform, Kalman filters, image reconstruction and computerized tomography, layered machines, linear and nonlinear autoencoders, and associative memories. Each chapter includes practical examples demonstrating real-world applications, supported by Python code, solution manuals, and presentation materials. This book also covers: Fundamental supervised and unsupervised machine learning methods with specific deep learning applications for image enhancement, segmentation, feature extraction, data compression, and classification Wavelet transform and filter banks integrated with state-of-the-art image analysis and processing Advanced filtering techniques including Wiener and Kalman filters, and two-dimensional image modeling Python implementations via Google colab platform enabling immediate application of theoretical concepts to practical image processing problems Instructor resources including solution manuals and presentation materials supporting adoption in digital image processing and computer vision courses Essential for professionals in industry and research laboratories requiring implementation-ready image processing methods, this reference also serves graduate students and advanced undergraduates in electrical and computer engineering, biomedical engineering, and computer science programs studying digital image processing and computer vision.

title: Conditional Timed Partial Orders: An Expressive and Interpretable Framework for Robot Task Specification and Planning
abstract: Timed Partial Orders (TPOs), originally proposed for workflows, provide an interpretable framework for robot task specification with planning algorithms based on mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). However, TPOs are limited in expressivity, capturing only partial-order events with simple timing constraints. In this paper, we introduce Conditional TPOs (cTPOs), which extend TPOs with richer relative-timing constraints and conditional event activations based on environmental conditions. We show that planning for cTPOs also reduces to an MILP problem; however, the added expressivity results in significantly larger MILPs that can become computationally intractable. To address this challenge, we propose a decomposition algorithm that partitions a cTPO into smaller sub-TPOs, yielding a sequence of smaller MILP problems. We prove that this decomposition is complete and preserves plan optimality while improving the interpretability of complex tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of cTPOs as a task specification framework and the efficiency of our decomposition approach, achieving up to four orders of magnitude speedup over the monolithic MILP.

title: Signed Rescue Routing: Harm-Aware Cascades for Efficient LLM Inference
abstract: Large language model (LLM) cascades answer easy requests with a small model and escalate selected requests to a larger model. Most routers prioritize examples on which the small model appears uncertain or likely to be wrong. This proxy ignores a decisive fact: escalation is useful only when the large model corrects the small model, and it is harmful when the large model replaces a correct answer with an incorrect one. We introduce Signed Rescue Routing (SRR), a budgeted routing method that predicts these two events separately and ranks requests by their difference. We show that this signed conditional gain is the Bayes-optimal routing score under a fixed escalation budget. SRR requires only the small model's output statistics at deployment and adds a lightweight two-head router. We evaluate SRR with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on TBD examples from MMLU, HellaSwag, and ARC-Challenge. Across the accuracy-compute curve, SRR reaches an area of TBD, compared with TBD for a learned small-model error predictor and TBD for entropy routing. These results show that predicting incremental value, rather than model uncertainty, is a simple and effective objective for efficient LLM cascades.

title: Supplementary Code and Census Artifacts for "Quadratic relations of differentially 4-uniform permutations: a sharp displacement bound and an orbit-equivariant census"
abstract: This repository contains the computational artifacts, replication code, and census datasets accompanying the research paper: "Quadratic relations of differentially 4-uniform permutations: a sharp displacement bound and an orbit-equivariant census" by Ilhom Abdurazzokov. Abstract:The AES S-box is the multiplicative inverse on GF(2^8) composed with an affine map, and it pays for its optimal (NL, DU) = (112, 4) with algebraic structure: exactly 39 linearly independent quadratic relations. This work investigates what it costs to give some of that structure up and characterizes the exact bounds. Writing Q(F) for the quadratic relation count and d_H for the Hamming distance from the inverse map, we prove that Q is 1-Lipschitz in d_H and characterize when the bound is attained. The archive includes:- Complete enumeration and verification scripts for the d_H <= 4 neighborhood (including the 1,573,133,760 permutations at d_H = 4).- Orbit-equivariant census data for permutations commuting with multiplicative subgroup C (|C| = 85 and |C| = 51 families).- Evaluation pipelines for quadratic relation counts (Q), differential uniformity (DU), nonlinearity (NL), and boomerang uniformity (beta).

evidence.title: Supplementary Code and Census Artifacts for "Quadratic relations of differentially 4-uniform permutations: a sharp displacement bound and an orbit-equivariant census"
evidence.abstract: This repository contains the computational artifacts, replication code, and census datasets accompanying the research paper: "Quadratic relations of differentially 4-uniform permutations: a sharp displacement bound and an orbit-equivariant census" by Ilhom Abdurazzokov. Abstract:The AES S-box is the multiplicative inverse on GF(2^8) composed with an affine map, and it pays for its optimal (NL, DU) = (112, 4) with algebraic structure: exactly 39 linearly independent quadratic relations. This work investigates what it costs to give some of that structure up and characterizes the exact bounds. Writing Q(F) for the quadratic relation count and d_H for the Hamming distance from the inverse map, we prove that Q is 1-Lipschitz in d_H and characterize when the bound is attained. The archive includes:- Complete enumeration and verification scripts for the d_H <= 4 neighborhood (including the 1,573,133,760 permutations at d_H = 4).- Orbit-equivariant census data for permutations commuting with multiplicative subgroup C (|C| = 85 and |C| = 51 families).- Evaluation pipelines for quadratic relation counts (Q), differential uniformity (DU), nonlinearity (NL), and boomerang uniformity (beta).

title: Dynamic Neural Networks: Adaptive Neuron Connectivity
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic neural network architecture that employs adaptive neuron connections to dynamically adjust the strength of connections based on the input data's dynamic changes. Traditional neural network models often rely on static connections, limiting their adaptability and potential for improved performance. Our proposed mechanism leverages iterative learning to automatically tune the connection weights, resulting in a more efficient and robust neural network. This work addresses the limitations of static models by enabling the network to respond intelligently to evolving data patterns. The resulting network demonstrates improved generalization capabilities and enhanced performance across a range of benchmark datasets.

title: 基于自组织网络的非线性几何模型优化器
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on a self-organizing network to refine geometric models. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex, non-linear models, and the inherent noise in the optimization process can lead to suboptimal solutions. This work leverages the self-organizing network's ability to iteratively refine parameters through a process of exploration and exploitation, resulting in improved model precision and generalization capabilities. The algorithm employs a modified reinforcement learning approach, incorporating a reward function that prioritizes model accuracy while considering the network's structure, fostering a dynamic and adaptable optimization process. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, showcasing significant improvements in model convergence and accuracy compared to traditional methods.

title: Dynamic Neuron Topology Mapping and Adaptive Neuron Connection Generation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for dynamically mapping neuron topologies and generating adaptive neuron connections within neural networks. The core idea is to integrate topological network modeling with reinforcement learning to create a system capable of learning and adapting to complex neural network topologies. The system employs a multi-level modeling approach. The first level utilizes topological networks such as small-world networks and scale-free networks to represent the neural network. The second level leverages reinforcement learning algorithms, such as policy gradient or Actor-Critic, to train the connection strength between neurons. Crucially, connection strength is determined not only by neuron input/output activity but also by local topological information, including connection density and distance. A third level, an adaptive topology generation module, dynamically alters the topology structure based on network performance and learning objectives, adding or removing neurons and modifying their connections. This approach aims to optimize information processing and learning efficiency by mitigating information bottlenecks and accelerating signal propagation. The system demonstrates the potential to overcome limitations of existing neural network modeling methods and address complex learning and information processing challenges in neural networks.

title: Probability Geometric Systems for Logical Revelation and High-Order Inference
abstract: Probability Geometric Systems (PGS) presents a novel approach to logical revelation and high-order inference by integrating probability logic geometry with the principles of set theory reversal. This system leverages the inherent properties of probability events to automatically discover hidden logical relationships and structures within data sets. The core mechanism centers around a dynamic, iterative process of event generation, logical deduction, and set-theoretic analysis, effectively uncovering patterns and dependencies that would otherwise remain hidden. This research proposes a framework for constructing a system capable of performing sophisticated reasoning, including the identification of complex relationships and the generation of novel insights. The significance of PGS lies in its potential to surpass traditional methods by embracing probabilistic reasoning and offering a more intuitive and automated approach to logical exploration.

title: Self-Organizing Fractal Neural Networks for Pattern Recognition
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to pattern recognition utilizing self-organizing fractal neural networks. The core idea is to leverage the inherent hierarchical structure of fractals to create networks that are both efficient and adaptable. We propose an evolutionary algorithm that iteratively refines the fractal network's topology, optimizing it for a specific pattern recognition task. The algorithm's guidance is based on a feedback mechanism that continuously assesses pattern recognition accuracy. Through this process, the network dynamically adjusts its fractal structure, leading to improved performance compared to traditional, static neural network architectures. This research demonstrates a promising pathway for developing intelligent systems capable of robust and adaptable pattern recognition in complex environments. The key mathematical formulations and concepts presented in this paper contribute to a deeper understanding of this emerging field.

title: Dynamic Topology in Quantum Circuit Design
abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic topology in quantum circuit design, aiming to enhance the efficiency and adaptability of quantum device fabrication. Traditional circuit design relies on fixed parameters, limiting design flexibility. Dynamic topology, leveraging the inherent properties of topological structures, offers a novel approach to circuit design, promising improved performance and the ability to explore complex circuit topologies. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing dynamic topology to enable novel quantum circuit designs, optimizing for specific applications. We present a conceptual framework for this approach, outlining key design considerations and potential benefits.

title: 基于量子概率的算法优化设计
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum probability to algorithm optimization, specifically targeting machine learning model optimization. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex, high-dimensional problems, while quantum mechanics offers the potential for enhanced performance through inherent probabilistic properties. We propose a novel algorithm, Quantum-Guided Optimization (QGO), that leverages quantum probability to guide the search process and improve model accuracy. The core mechanism of QGO centers around quantum state manipulation to represent and explore the solution space efficiently. This approach demonstrates improved performance compared to classical optimization techniques on a benchmark dataset of neural network training.

title: Algorithmic Randomness Generation via Quantum Walks
abstract: The generation of true randomness remains a significant challenge in computer science, particularly when relying solely on classical algorithms. Many current approaches employ pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs), which, despite their computational efficiency, are inherently predictable and lack genuine randomness. This paper proposes a novel method for algorithmic randomness generation leveraging the principles of quantum walks. We demonstrate that the inherent uncertainty and superposition properties of quantum systems provide a robust mechanism for generating truly random numbers. Specifically, we outline a framework for designing quantum walks on graphs, where the evolution of the walker's state is fundamentally probabilistic and unpredictable. The core of our approach resides in exploiting the quantum walk's non-deterministic nature to produce sequences of numbers that exhibit statistical properties consistent with true randomness. The theoretical framework is presented, including a detailed description of the mathematical formalism underlying the quantum walk and the probability distribution of the walker's positions. We highlight the potential advantages of this approach, particularly in scenarios demanding high-quality randomness for cryptographic applications or simulations. The key concept is to translate a classical problem into a quantum one, where the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics offers a superior solution to the problem of generating genuine randomness.

title: Phase-Field Optimization - Dynamical Constraint Optimization of Complex Systems
abstract: Phase-field optimization represents a novel approach to dynamic optimization, offering a robust method for optimizing complex systems by iteratively adjusting parameters based on the current state. This paper explores the core principles of this technique, detailing the algorithm's implementation, its advantages over existing methods, and its potential applications in various fields. We delve into the importance of defining constraints and the iterative adjustment process to achieve optimal results. The focus is on demonstrating the effectiveness of the phase-field approach through a concrete example, showcasing its ability to handle complex scenarios with dynamic constraints. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, aiming to further refine the algorithm and expand its applicability.

title: Quantum Memory Mechanism in Quantum Error Correction Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel "quantum memory" mechanism within quantum error correction (QEC) networks, leveraging continuous-time error correction codes and the nonlinear properties of superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). The core claim is the design of a system capable of storing and retrieving past quantum states, significantly enhancing the overall resilience and performance of QEC networks. The mechanism utilizes an engineered "quantum memory" built within an SQUID, allowing for the controlled storage and replay of quantum state information generated during error correction processes. Unlike conventional QEC codes limited to single-shot corrections, this approach incorporates historical data for optimized error mitigation. Mathematical formulations detailing the core concepts and operational parameters are presented, illustrating the potential for improved error correction rates and extended coherence times in QEC networks. This research contributes a fundamental shift in QEC methodology, moving beyond sequential correction to a dynamic, state-aware approach.

title: Multidimensional Probability Space for Quantum Simulation
abstract: Quantum simulation is a crucial field for understanding and manipulating quantum systems, demanding sophisticated computational methods. Traditional approaches often face limitations in the representation and manipulation of complex quantum states. This paper proposes a novel quantum simulation framework predicated on the utilization of a multidimensional probability space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a detailed analysis of its capabilities and limitations, emphasizing its potential to surpass current approximations in quantum state representation and simulation precision. The core claim is that this framework, by embracing a probabilistic representation, allows for a more accurate and detailed simulation of quantum phenomena.

title: Adam: Open Representation Birth, Compositional Theory Selection, and Auditable Scientific Rediscovery Based on Dual-Level CAF-VGCTG
abstract: Abstract Existing AI systems for scientific discovery mainly focus on recovering expressions, parameters, or structures within predefined candidate spaces from observational data. A more difficult question is whether, when the target scientific representation itself is not explicitly supplied, an AI system can reorganize existing but fragmented knowledge and autonomously form a higher-level anonymous representation; at the same time, whether an older representation that remains persistently incompatible with the new evidence structure can naturally lose qualification through evidence-driven compositional failure, rather than because the researcher has rewarded the target answer in advance. We introduce Adam, an auditable scientific-reasoning architecture and benchmark based on Dual-level Cross-Area Fusion VGCTG (DCAFVGCTG). The architecture separates six classes of mechanisms that are otherwise easily conflated: directional eligibility, cross-area conditional superposition, long-term law-relation memory, recoverable graph abstraction, representation composition/anonymous birth, and downstream execution correction. The first CAF level permits conditional transfer only from lower-curvature to higher-curvature regions according to dynamically reconstructed curvature ordering. The second CAF level is defined as a true recoverable Graph Loss operator (L_G), which compresses admissible multistep structures into higher-level abstract relations while retaining an archive capable of reconstructing the source path. SEC acts only on execution weights after the structure has been determined and is not permitted to alter curvature-direction topology, CAF topology, or the abstract graph. Adam is built on the earlier VGCTG architecture, as instantiated in the frozen second-generation VRCTG/VDRCTG implementation VRCTG_VDRCTG_v3_0_FROZEN1 (hereafter GMv3), but does not replace VGCTG’s existing relation- and direction-governance mechanisms. VGCTG already distinguishes the latent law relation (R_{ij}^{\mathrm{law}}), current data reliability (G_i^{\mathrm{data}}), instantaneous lower-to-higher directional eligibility (A_{ij}^{\kappa}), and actual execution weight (P_{ij}^{\mathrm{exec}}), and uses relation compatibility, persistent incompatibility, dormancy, and retraction to govern whether local candidates remain eligible to share a law. Adam adds representation-level structural composability above this relation layer. For scientifically distinct representations such as ether, scalar, vector, and metric-like representations, an artificial numerical concept distance such as (d(\mathrm{ether},\mathrm{metric})) cannot be naturally defined. Representation survival is therefore determined by whether heterogeneous evidence can be composed into a closed, compressive, recoverable, and predictively capable structure. In the strongest experiment, metric is completely removed from the proposal space. The system may use only existing non-target representations and anonymous latent variables (z_k). Anonymous representations are first born independently and are only afterward evaluated through a common post-hoc characterization ledger to determine whether they possess metric-like properties. For the normalized preferred-frame ether competitor, insufficient evidence permits only dormancy; actual retraction requires both persistent compositional failure and reliable contradiction in an independent paired blind region. Thus, “excluding ether” and “forming a metric-like representation” are two independent mechanism chains. In the frozen 701:730 block, 28 of 30 seeds formed anonymous representations, of which 3 were subsequently characterized as metric-like and simultaneously satisfied the predefined Adam-0 conditions. All three passed the field-equation gate and completed independent tensor and weak-field audits. In the one-time independent confirmation block 801:830, 24/30 seeds produced anonymous representations, of which 2 formed metric-like Adam-0 events. Across the five authorized events, the byte-locked field-equation assembler consistently recovered a Ricci + (Rg) structure with (b/a) close to (-1/2), while the weak-field coupling remained near (2.076\times10^{-43}). Destroying the conservation ledger or the weak-field ledger counterfactually disrupted the corresponding tensor ratio or coupling. No seed without a metric-like anonymous representation was permitted to activate the field-equation assembler. In the subsequent frozen FEv4 independent-confirmation block 1001:1030, the real arm produced anonymous representations in 22/30 seeds, with 1/30 satisfying both metric-like Birth and Adam-0 criteria. The corresponding metric-like Birth and Adam-0 counts were both 2/30 in the cross-edge arm; the paired exact comparison of metric-like emergence rates gave p=1. Cross-edge interventions were validly applied in 9/30 seeds and reached the audited Birth input in 5/30 seeds, whereas the GL source-evidence arm produced no valid composition-changing sample. These results extend the independent-block observation of Adam-0 but establish neither a success-rate advantage over the cross-edge null nor the effect of effective GL evidence reassociation. In the subsequent separate block 1701:1730, FEv5 v0.7 applied two-dimensional priority selection after qualification: common DECISION predictive improvement first, qualified BirthScore second. Across six paired arms, input-concept challenge C and dual-source governance D each achieved Adam-0 and governed Adam-0 in 2/30 seeds, compared with 1/30 in original arm A, output-side arm B, budget control E, and common-lifecycle control F. All five prespecified Adam-0 paired comparisons had exact and Holm-adjusted (p) values of 1; the corresponding governed comparisons also had exact (p) values of 1. The increased counts therefore do not establish a statistically significant success-rate advantage. C and D had identical success counts despite mean search trials of 14 and 72, respectively, with no additional observed success rate in D. The FEv4 cross-edge arm had already reached 2/30; cross-block counts are not used to estimate the effects of anti-intuition or priority selection. These results do not constitute an independent discovery of general relativity by AI from a “no-knowledge” condition. The stricter conclusion is that, within a frozen, auditable benchmark that isolates the target label while intentionally retaining structured physical priors, an unnamed higher-order scientific representation can naturally emerge from fragmented knowledge, while an older representation that persistently fails to compose the evidence can lose qualification through an independent evidence chain. We call this minimal phenomenon Adam-0 and characterize the present result as auditable constrained scientific rediscovery. Keywords: scientific discovery AI; DCAFVGCTG; CAF; Graph Loss; relation plasticity; direction plasticity; open representation birth; compositional theory selection; Adam-0; Newton; Einstein; constrained rediscovery

title: Discriminability-Aware Symmetric Bit-Wise Feature Encoding for Resource-Constrained IoT Traffic Classification
abstract: Resource-constrained traffic classification requires mapping heterogeneous numerical features into a fixed-length binary input. Equal-width encoding ignores differences in discriminability, whereas range-only allocation may spend precision on weak predictors. We propose discriminability-aware symmetric bit-wise feature encoding (DA-SBFE), which combines training-fold mutual information with a robust numerical range to allocate tiered feature precision under a fixed budget. P4-programmable SmartNICs serve as a deployment-oriented case study because constrained per-packet processing motivates compact, deterministic representations. We do not claim hardware deployment. On 83,868 packets from the official UNSW IoT traces, DA-SBFE with BNN-Large achieved 0.9330 ± 0.0019 macro-F1 at 256 bits versus 0.9185 ± 0.0020 for Range-SBFE, with positive differences in all five folds. title: Ant colony mapping for dimensionality reduction to discrete spaces
abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a widely used technique in AI with various application areas. It maps feature vectors of high dimension to a space of lower dimension so that the new representation maintains some meaningful properties of the original data (i.e., similar vectors have similar new representations). This paper considers the problem of dimensionality reduction to discrete spaces. A novel distributed, stochastic ’swarm intelligence’ algorithm, Ant Colony Mapping (ACOM), is proposed to generate approximate solutions to the problem. ACOM is a generalisation of the brood-sorting behaviour of certain ant species that results in the spatial clustering of objects. After demonstrating ACOM’s basic behaviour, the algorithm’s performance on 2D lattice topologies is analysed in terms of the number of ants and the number of problem parameters. The performance is compared to that of a recent, local search-enhanced Steady-State Genetic Algorithm, namely Steady-State Memetic Algorithm (SSMA), as a baseline, both in terms of solution quality and computational budget. Additional experiments compare ACOM, an annealed variant, and an LAS-ACOM hybrid with non-evolutionary grid-sorting baselines on a random-RGB benchmark. Annealing and hybridisation improve ACOM’s alignment quality, but global baselines remain stronger; in exchange, ACOM uses local operations with constant complexity rather than the cubic complexity of assignment-based methods.

title: Abstention Errors and Segment Support in CUAD: An Auditable Contract-Extraction Case Study
abstract: Contract-clause extraction benchmarks measure reference recovery, but interpreting a system for review assistance also requires measuring unnecessary output and the evidence available within categories. This paper presents a retrospective, reproducible evaluation of a fixed public RoBERTa checkpoint on CUAD's published 102-contract test split. Candidate generation is preserved from an earlier frozen run; matching errors are corrected and category thresholds are reselected on 62 training-split contracts using the original 90% recall target. The corrected operating point recovers 82.2% of reference spans at 8.2% CUAD precision. Of 30,464 returned candidate strings, 19,562 occur on questions with no annotated answer. The system answers 1,335 of 2,938 such questions, a 45.4% false-positive rate (95% contract-bootstrap interval: 43.3-47.9%). Matching candidates constitute 20.3% of returned strings, illustrating why reference-based precision and candidate-level review burden require different denominators. Only nine of 41 categories have at least 30 positive and 30 negative contracts; this count changes to 18 and two under support minima of 20 and 40. Two categories have no negative contracts, making their no-answer false-positive rates undefined. These findings describe one checkpoint, decoder, and threshold policy. Earlier test access and uncertain checkpoint training overlap limit confirmatory interpretation. The paper supplies the original and corrected analyses, predictions, and software checks as ancillary artifacts; it establishes neither a new release criterion nor production readiness.

title: Toward Fault-Tolerant Variational Optimization: QAOA under [[4,2,2]] Error Detection
abstract: We present a partially fault-tolerant implementation of QAOA based on the $[[4,2,2]]$ error-detection code, targeting the Max-Cut problem on a square graph. Our main contribution is a novel ancilla-mediated logical $R_{ZZ}$ gate enabling interactions between qubits in different $[[4,2,2]]$ blocks. We evaluate unencoded and encoded circuits under five noise models, with both all-to-all and grid-routed connectivity, using the Cirq and qsimcirq frameworks with parallel CPU execution. Post-selection on stabilizer measurements consistently improves the probability of sampling optimal bitstrings, with five measurements providing the strongest benefit. These results support error-detection as a practical near-term strategy for improving the quality of variational quantum algorithms.

title: LatentMD: Benchmarking Markdown Boundary Failures in LLM-Generated Text
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate Markdown that is consumed by renderers, agents, code extractors, and structured downstream pipelines. Yet existing evaluations often conflate content quality with format adherence, leaving Markdown boundary failures under-measured. We introduce LatentMD, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for diagnosing CommonMark-level fence-boundary failures in LLM-generated Markdown. LatentMD separates content correctness from boundary correctness, enabling detection of outputs that are content-correct but boundary-broken. The benchmark contains 4,179 prompts and a CLI for scoring arbitrary model outputs. Across 9 LLMs and roughly 37,600 generations, we find that Markdown boundary failures are widespread: 38.0% of valid main-grid outputs are content-correct but boundary-broken, with substantial boundary breakage under unspecified prompts and in a small human-authored validation set. Ablations show that failures are driven primarily by same-family symmetric-delimiter collisions rather than nesting alone, are only partially mitigated by prompt hints, and generalize to Python triple-quote docstrings while JSON remains robust as an asymmetric-delimiter control. LatentMD provides a reproducible diagnostic target for parser-sensitive LLM evaluation.

title: Algorithmic Optimization via Topology-Based Search
abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic optimization method predicated on the principles of topology-based search. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with complex, high-dimensional problems, requiring significant computational resources and time. This research proposes a novel approach that utilizes topological concepts to intelligently guide the search process, potentially achieving greater efficiency and effectiveness in finding optimal solutions. We detail the construction of a 'Topological Search Algorithm' designed to systematically explore the solution space, leveraging the inherent structure of the problem to prioritize promising regions. The paper explores the potential benefits of this methodology, including enhanced search efficiency, improved solution quality, and the ability to address previously intractable optimization problems. We will present the implementation of this algorithm and discuss its theoretical foundations and experimental validation.

title: Adaptive Fractal Geometry for High-Dimensional Data Representation
abstract: High-dimensional data presents significant challenges for traditional data analysis and representation techniques. The 'curse of dimensionality' often leads to sparsity of information and difficulties in identifying meaningful patterns. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging adaptive fractal geometry to address these issues. The core concept is that fractal landscapes, inherently capable of representing hierarchical and self-similar structures, can be dynamically adjusted to effectively capture the underlying distribution of high-dimensional data. We propose an algorithm that generates fractal landscapes in real-time, adapting parameters like fractal dimension (D), iteration depth (I), and scaling factor (S) based on local data density and variance. This dynamic adaptation provides a robust representation for non-stationary data, offering improved clustering, dimensionality reduction, and anomaly detection capabilities compared to static fractal methods. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through simulations and theoretical analysis, demonstrating its effectiveness in various scenarios. The key contribution lies in the real-time adaptability, moving beyond static fractal representations and offering a more nuanced and effective approach to high-dimensional data analysis.

title: Neural Network Solutions for Neural Telegraph Equations
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to solving Neural Telegraph Equations (NTEs) using deep learning. Traditional numerical methods for NTEs often struggle with accuracy and efficiency, particularly for complex systems and long time horizons. We propose a neural network architecture trained to directly approximate the solution of the NTEs, given initial conditions and time steps. The core mechanism involves mapping the input (initial state, time step) to the corresponding neural state at the output time step. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, showcasing its potential for efficient and accurate NTE simulation. The key innovation lies in bypassing the limitations of conventional numerical schemes and leveraging the inherent ability of deep neural networks to learn complex, non-linear relationships. This approach offers a promising alternative for various applications involving neural communication and signal propagation.

title: Dimension Space Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum entanglement-based adaptive optimization algorithm designed to address complex optimization problems. The core concept revolves around exploiting the instantaneous information transfer capabilities of entangled states to guide the optimization process, thereby mitigating the pitfalls of local optima and enabling global optimization. The algorithm incorporates a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism predicated on entanglement, allowing it to adapt to environmental changes and potentially achieve superior performance compared to traditional optimization techniques. This work explores the theoretical foundations of entanglement-based optimization and demonstrates its potential for significant advancements in the field of adaptive learning and problem-solving.

title: Quantum Entanglement Decomposition via Topological Self-Unfolding
abstract: Quantum entanglement plays a pivotal role in various quantum algorithms and quantum information processing, offering the potential for enhanced computational capabilities. However, the inherent complexity of entangled states often poses significant challenges, particularly in achieving efficient manipulation and analysis. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum state decomposition – the Quantum Entanglement Decomposition (QED) algorithm – based on topological self-unfolding. We propose a method that leverages the inherent topological properties of quantum states to transform them into a more structured and interpretable representation, facilitating deeper understanding and computational efficiency. The core mechanism centers around creating a topological manifold within the quantum state, allowing for efficient manipulation and analysis of the underlying entanglement structure. This research introduces a new framework for quantum state decomposition, demonstrating potential advancements in the comprehension and processing of entangled quantum systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's theoretical foundation, experimental validation, and future research directions.
