title: Dynamic Bayesian Network Inference with Compressed Sensing Techniques
abstract: This paper investigates the application of compressed sensing techniques to accelerate Bayesian network inference, particularly within the context of dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). Traditional Bayesian network inference methods often suffer from computational bottlenecks, especially when dealing with large and complex networks. The core idea presented here is to leverage the principles of compressed sensing – specifically, sparsity and incoherence – to dramatically reduce the computational burden of inference. We explore how compressed sensing can be integrated into the inference process, focusing on reducing the number of samples needed to accurately estimate network parameters. The approach is demonstrated through a theoretical framework, outlining the key mathematical formulations and the underlying principles. The primary focus is on the reduction of the computational complexity associated with message passing algorithms commonly used in DBN inference. The work aims to provide a viable pathway toward real-time inference in large-scale dynamic systems by offering a computationally efficient alternative. This research contributes to the growing field of hybrid Bayesian modeling and compressed sensing, with potential applications in areas such as sensor networks, time series analysis, and predictive maintenance.

title: Quantum-Based Unsupervised Feature Representation Learning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing for unsupervised feature representation learning. Traditional unsupervised methods often rely on manually designed feature extraction algorithms, limiting their applicability to complex datasets. We propose a novel approach leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum gate operations to achieve unsupervised feature extraction directly from raw data. This approach aims to enhance the generalization capability and robustness of machine learning models. The core idea involves constructing a quantum circuit-based model that implicitly maps input data and extracts relevant features through quantum entanglement and gate operations. We present a theoretical framework outlining the methodology and discuss the potential benefits and challenges of this emerging field. The primary goal is to demonstrate that quantum computing offers a fundamentally different paradigm for unsupervised learning, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical approaches. ---

title: Quantum Entangled Learning: A Probabilistic Structure Optimization Framework
abstract: Quantum Entangled Learning (QEL) offers a novel approach to machine learning, leveraging quantum entanglement to enhance learning efficiency and generalization ability. This paper proposes a new probabilistic structure optimization framework for QEL, focusing on the dynamic adjustment of entanglement patterns to adapt to varying data types and task specifications. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through a series of simulations and experiments, showcasing improved learning speed and robustness across diverse datasets. The core mechanism involves integrating probability logic with a customizable entanglement model, enabling tailored optimization strategies. The resulting system exhibits superior performance compared to existing methods, representing a significant advancement in the application of quantum principles to machine learning.

title: 基于图神经网络的符号逻辑推理
abstract: This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to symbolic logic reasoning. Traditional methods for symbolic logic inference often rely on heuristic algorithms and rule engines, which can be inefficient, particularly for complex logical systems. We propose a novel framework that leverages the structural representation capabilities of GNNs to model and solve symbolic logic problems effectively. The core idea involves transforming symbolic logic formulas into graph structures, enabling GNNs to learn embeddings that capture the relationships within the logic. These embeddings are then utilized to perform logical inference tasks, such as deriving new formulas or validating formula validity. This approach offers a potentially more scalable and efficient solution compared to existing methods. The key contributions of this work lie in the integration of graph representation learning with symbolic logic reasoning, providing a new computational paradigm for this long-standing problem.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum information theory to revolutionize chemical design and analysis. We propose a novel framework leveraging the inherent topological properties of molecules and their interactions to enable efficient probabilistic calculations and data compression. The core mechanism centers around directly applying the topology of molecules to quantum computation, utilizing quantum-enhanced topological encoding, and exploring its implications for accelerated data processing. This approach distinguishes itself from traditional quantum information theory by focusing on the structural dynamics of molecules, offering a pathway to surpass current computational limitations. We demonstrate the feasibility of this design through conceptual analysis and preliminary simulations, highlighting its potential for groundbreaking advancements in chemical modeling and optimization.

We demonstrate the feasibility of this design through conceptual analysis and preliminary simulations, highlighting its potential for groundbreaking advancements in chemical modeling and optimization.

title: Title: Non-Deterministic Quantum State Evolution & Reconstruction
abstract: Quantum state evolution is a fundamental challenge in quantum information processing, particularly when dealing with imperfect measurements and noisy environments. The inherent uncertainty in quantum measurements necessitates strategies for robust state reconstruction. This paper introduces a novel method for reconstructing quantum states from non-deterministic evolution, employing quantum error correction to significantly enhance fidelity. The core mechanism centers around a state reconstruction algorithm predicated on quantum error correction principles, designed to mitigate the effects of measurement errors during the initial state preparation phase. The research explores a practical implementation of this algorithm, demonstrating its ability to recover information with improved accuracy compared to conventional methods, particularly under challenging conditions. We address the core claim that this method offers a pathway to robust state reconstruction from imperfect measurement, leveraging the power of quantum error correction.

title: Title: Dynamical Constraint Optimization of Quantum Systems (DCOS) - Efficiently Optimizing Complex Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamical Constraint Optimization of Quantum Systems (DCOS), a novel algorithm for efficiently optimizing complex quantum algorithms. Traditional methods for optimizing quantum algorithms often involve iterative adjustments of parameters, which can be time-consuming and require significant manual intervention. DCOS leverages dynamic constraints to guide the optimization process, offering a more streamlined and automated approach. The core mechanism involves iteratively adjusting parameters based on the current state of a quantum system, effectively minimizing the algorithm's cost function. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis and a practical implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of DCOS in optimizing several key quantum algorithms. The paper details the algorithm's design, its performance compared to existing methods, and discusses potential future directions for research and development. The primary goal is to provide a robust and scalable solution for optimizing complex quantum computations, reducing the burden on researchers and developers.

title: Dynamic Key Management in Quantum Cryptography
abstract: Quantum cryptography offers unprecedented security by utilizing the laws of quantum mechanics to encrypt and transmit information. However, the inherent fragility of quantum states necessitates sophisticated key management strategies. This paper presents a novel dynamic key management algorithm for quantum cryptography, designed to automatically adjust key parameters based on evolving security requirements. We propose a method that leverages the inherent dynamism of quantum states to achieve enhanced security through continuous key adaptation. The algorithm incorporates a feedback loop that monitors security threats and dynamically modifies key variables to maintain optimal security levels. This approach aims to surpass the limitations of static key management systems, contributing to a more resilient and adaptable quantum cryptographic infrastructure. This research explores the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this dynamic key adjustment approach, demonstrating its potential to significantly bolster the security posture of quantum communication systems.

title: Neural Network Self-Organization Driven by Information Entropy in Neuron Models
abstract: This research investigates the potential for information entropy to drive self-organization within neuron models and, consequently, within artificial neural networks. The core claim posits that fluctuations in information entropy within a neuron network can induce a dynamic process of self-organization, leading to enhanced information encoding and transmission. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a multi-layered neuron network model, continuously monitoring the entropy values of individual neurons and their connections, and leveraging the entropy increase principle alongside neuronal interactions. This process facilitates the self-organization of entropy distributions, ultimately optimizing the network's structure and functionality. Mathematical modeling explores the dynamics of entropy and its influence on network connectivity. The research contributes a novel approach to neural network design by explicitly incorporating entropy as a fundamental driver of self-organization, offering a potential pathway to more efficient and adaptive neural architectures. The study examines the theoretical underpinnings of this phenomenon and outlines a framework for future investigation.

title: Based on Chaos, Quantum Computing Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of incorporating chaos theory and quantum computing into algorithm design optimization for quantum computation. The core claim is that a novel algorithm framework, leveraging the unique properties of chaos, can significantly enhance the efficiency and stability of quantum computations. The research explores a method for dynamically adjusting quantum parameters based on chaotic dynamics, thereby mitigating errors and improving the likelihood of finding optimal solutions. The paper details the design of a specialized optimization loop, incorporating elements of stochasticity and sensitivity analysis, that responds to the inherent fluctuations within the quantum system. The benefits of this approach are anticipated to include increased computational speed and improved error mitigation. This work represents a significant step toward a more robust and adaptive approach to quantum algorithm design.

title: Artifact for Article: Extending Deductive Verification of SYCL in VerCors with Sub-groups
abstract: Artifact for article "Extending Deductive Verification of SYCL in VerCors with Sub-groups" submitted to the STTT journal. For a full description on how to use the artifact, please see the README.md file. The artifact contains a docker image of the VerCors tool (with the described SYCL support) and documentation. Abstract of Article: SYCL is a C++ programming model for the development of heterogeneous programs. It uses the concept of kernels, where multiple instances of a computation are executed concurrently on a computing unit. This concurrency entails that the set of possible program behaviours can be of considerable size, which makes these programs error-prone. Formal verification could be used to ensure the correctness of all these possible program behaviours. In this article, SYCL support is added to VerCors, a formal verification tool for concurrent software, by encoding SYCL constructs into VerCors' internal language COL. To the extent of our knowledge, this is the first deductive verification tool for SYCL. We show how SYCL's basic- and ND-range kernels are encoded, along with the encoding and challenges related to scheduling kernels and the execution order of those kernels. Next, we discuss how SYCL's buffers and data accessors are encoded, focusing on the challenges related to it, in particular enabling memory transfer between host and device. Finally, we dicuss the encoding for sub-groups and sub-group-intrinsic functions. The usability of the added SYCL support and how it was evaluated are discussed as well.

title: Geometric interpretation of the triality relation in bipartite quantum systems
abstract: Abstract We investigate quantum correlations and coherence in bipartite systems using the universal triality relation that connects coherence, predictability, and entanglement. The geometric structure underlying entanglement in bipartite two-qubit and two-qutrit systems is analyzed using wedge products of post-measurement vectors. For two-qubit states, concurrence emerges naturally as the area spanned by the post-measurement vectors, while in qutrit systems the generalized I-concurrence is associated with higher-dimensional geometric structures formed by multiple wedge products. We further analyze the relationship between wedge products, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors of correlated systems and discuss the universality of the triality relation in arbitrary dimensions. Our results provide a geometric interpretation of entanglement in d -dimensional cases and reveal a hierarchical structure connecting low- and high-dimensional quantum systems.

title: A stage-selective transfer learning framework for small-sample quality prediction in injection molding
abstract: In small-sample injection molding quality prediction, limited target-domain data hinder stable model training, motivating transfer learning from source-domain data. However, injection molding is a multi-stage dynamic process in which injection, packing, and cooling differ in quality relevance and cross-domain feature matching, so source-domain knowledge does not have equal transfer value across stages. Existing transfer learning methods mainly rely on model parameter transfer or global feature alignment, which obscures stage-wise transfer value and dilutes target-domain-specific information. To address these limitations, this study proposes a stage-selective transfer learning framework that treats process stages as the basic transfer units. Stage transferability is evaluated by matching source-domain stage prototypes with target-domain shared features and integrated with target-domain stage importance to generate stage-selective weights. A target-domain-specific stage branch preserves intrinsic responses, while stage-level and multi-space distribution alignment constraints reduce cross-domain discrepancies. A discrepancy-aware stage attenuation mechanism further suppresses transfer and alignment contributions from severely mismatched source-domain stages. Experiments on real-world injection molding datasets show that common backbone models achieve R 2 improvements of 10.54 %–16.91 % under random splitting and 9.48 %–19.93 % under chronological splitting. Fixed-sample-size experiments confirm consistent transfer gains with only 10–100 labeled target-domain training samples, while controlled severe stage-mismatch tests demonstrate that the attenuation mechanism recovers approximately 75 % of the induced R 2 loss.

title: Modern Image Classification‐Layered Machines
abstract: The hierarchical structure of deep neural networks is neurobiologically inspired by the simple and complex cells of the visual cortex. Their layered architecture facilitates automated feature extraction, enabling pattern recognition that is invariant to translation, rotation, scaling, illumination, and distortion. This chapter introduces foundational layered machines, including Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), covering their full training stages via error back-propagation algorithm. Furthermore, it covers various loss functions and learning algorithms for deep CNNs. The chapter also extends the unsupervised competitive learning from Chapter 17 to Self-Organizing Feature Maps (SOFMs) and variants of Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ). Practical considerations for efficient training of these networks are provided. Many realistic examples of these machines are included for various DIP tasks. The chapter ends with computer projects and challenging problems.

title: Beyond the Matrix Sign: Quadratic Spectral Descent
abstract: Muon emerges as a strong competitor of the AdamW for LLM pretraining, because the matrix-wise update it employs can potentially incur smaller second-order penalty than the once dominating AdamW, which performs coordinate-wise update. However, the spectral flattening procedure in Muon is quite debatable since it discards the spectral amplitude information totally. To seek for better spectral allocation (and the associated spectral subspace), we propose to solve the quadratic model of loss function under the spectral norm constraint \textit{directly} (i.e., in a genuinely Newtonian way) and thus obtaining the Quadratic Spectral Descent (QSD) algorithm. In contrast, many existing curvature-aware methods either exploit the second-order information in an \textit{implicit} way by changing the weight update geometry (such as Mousse, FISMO) or rely on strong assumptions (such as the weight displacement isotropy assumption in Newton-Muon). QSD's potential advantage over these methods is best illustrated in the isotropic curvature scenario, where Mousse, FISMO and Newton-Muon all reduce to Muon while the spectral allocation in QSD is still \textit{non-flat} (since the spectral allocation in QSD depends on the \textit{gradient to curvature ratio}). Meanwhile, to control the complexity of QSD, we employ inversion-free K-FAC and \textit{online} Frank-Wolfe update which is essentially a matrix sign operator. Overall, the complexity increase can be rather mild. Experiments on GPT pre-training show that QSD consistently improves validation loss over Muon and recent Muon variants, while achieving up to an $8.49\%$ wall-clock speedup at matched validation loss.

title: Cat-Code-Protected Controlled Quantum Communication via Non-Local CNOT Gates over Star Quantum Networks
abstract: Controlled quantum communication enables secure state transfer between a sender and receiver with the assistance of one or more controllers. However, practical implementation over optical fibre networks is severely hindered by amplitude damping, which reduces fidelity exponentially with distance. We address this challenge by combining two powerful techniques: cat-state encoding for error correction and optimal non-local CNOT gates for distributed gate implementation. The protocol eliminates the need for the physical position qubit itself to travel through the optical fibre, reducing damping events. We show, through density-matrix simulations, that our cat-code-protected protocol with a non-local CNOT operation achieves higher fidelity at 50 km, significantly outperforming the standard protocol. We analyse the protocol's security against beam-splitter attacks and show that CHSH tests provide security against beam-splitter attacks on the distributed entanglement resource despite the cat code's error correction. Our results establish that cat-code-protected controlled quantum communication is feasible with current technology and structurally extensible to multiple controllers, providing a theoretical framework for studying error-corrected controlled quantum communication over long-distance star quantum networks.

title: Task-dependent model selection for structured extraction from multilingual non-English clinical records
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate task-dependent selection of local and cloud models for structured extraction from multilingual non-English stroke discharge summaries, distinguishing entity detection, record assembly, and raw-document processing. Methods This retrospective system evaluation compared multilingual encoders, locally fine-tuned Qwen3-4B models, and zero-shot GPT-5.5. Primary test cohorts comprised 332 section cases, 149 medication cases with 2,475 reference records after identity-based exclusions, and 191 laboratory cases. Outcomes were section-span F1, drug-name F1, normalized seven-field record recovery, test-name F1, and laboratory quintuple F1. Paired human comparisons used a common second-annotator reference on 50 cases per task. Saved cascade outputs were compared with curated-section controls using document-bootstrap intervals. Results Section F1 was 0.919 for the encoder, 0.926 for GPT-5.5, and 0.932 for Qwen. GPT-5.5 led medication detection (0.966 versus 0.940 for Qwen), whereas Qwen led normalized medication recovery (0.381 versus 0.311; difference 0.070, 95% CI 0.026–0.114) and laboratory quintuple F1 (0.892 versus 0.822). With matched inference stacks, medication recovery declined from 0.377 on curated inputs to 0.204 for single-window and 0.246 for all-block cascades; quintuple F1 on the original laboratory cohort declined from 0.898 to 0.811. Corpus-wide extraction processed 193,101 summaries in 13.3 H100 GPU-hours. Conclusion Local models achieved strong detection performance without frontier-scale inference in this setting. Fine-tuned local LLMs were advantageous for record assembly under the evaluated recipes; annotation conventions, normalization, and upstream section extraction remained important constraints.

title: Quantum Geometry Information Encoding for High-Dimensional Data Compression and Analysis
abstract: Quantum Geometry Information Encoding (QGIEC) is a novel approach to data compression and analysis leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement and superposition. This paper presents a method that encodes high-dimensional data within quantum bits (qubits) using quantum entanglement and superposition, aiming to achieve significantly improved compression efficiency and enhanced data analysis capabilities compared to existing techniques. The core mechanism centers around the creation of entangled states that represent data, enabling efficient manipulation and decoding through quantum algorithms. The study demonstrates the practical feasibility of QGIEC through simulations and preliminary experiments, highlighting its potential to revolutionize data storage and processing.

title: ECPC Supplementary Materials and Reproducibility Artifact for Evidence-Carrying Portability Contracts
abstract: Supplementary materials and executable reproducibility artifact supporting the manuscript "Evidence-Carrying Portability Contracts for Compiler Security Instrumentation: Differential Reconstruction of Shadow Call Stack Protocols" (manuscript information-4490441). Supplementary File S1 provides the ECPC operational specification, evidence ledger, rule-change log, and reproduction guide. Supplementary File S2 provides the version 2.1.0 standard-library Python model, eight version-pinned descriptors, authoritative rule catalogue, frozen expectation fixture, semantic tests, provenance ledger, generated matrices and witnesses, benchmark, checksums, license, and citation metadata. A fresh reference execution passes 30 semantic tests. The Compact TLS x86_64 case remains a specified design because its implementation source is unavailable; the deposit contains no performance or production-readiness claim for that configuration.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Correction: An Adaptive Error Correction Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum state correction algorithm designed to significantly enhance the robustness and efficiency of quantum information processing and quantum computation. Traditional error correction methods often rely on pre-computed error correction matrices, limiting their adaptability. Our approach leverages the inherent dynamic nature of quantum states to proactively detect and correct errors, overcoming the limitations of conventional techniques. The core mechanism involves a dynamically adapting quantum state transformation, enabling a more resilient and efficient error correction process. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach to improve the performance and reliability of quantum systems.

title: Cognitive Architecture and Evolutionary Algorithms: Towards Autonomous Learning Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence development by integrating cognitive architecture and evolutionary algorithms. The core claim is that a system combining these two paradigms can effectively facilitate autonomous learning and adaptation in AI agents. The proposed mechanism involves leveraging cognitive architecture's capabilities for knowledge representation and inference alongside the evolutionary algorithm's strengths in exploration and optimization. This hybrid system aims to overcome the limitations of traditional AI approaches that often rely on pre-programmed rules or supervised learning, which struggle with complex, dynamic environments. The presented framework offers a pathway to create more robust and flexible AI systems capable of continuous learning and adaptation without explicit human intervention. The system's architecture is described, along with key components and their interactions, outlining a potential design for a self-improving AI agent. Further research directions and potential challenges are also discussed.

title: Title: Dynamic Geometry for Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Dynamic Geometry for Adaptive Machine Learning addresses the limitations of static machine learning models by introducing a mechanism for dynamically adjusting geometric properties during training. This novel approach leverages quantum annealing to optimize for robustness and efficiency, ultimately enhancing generalization performance. This paper explores the potential of quantum annealing as a tool for optimizing model geometry, presenting a framework for dynamically adjusting key parameters to improve model resilience and accelerate learning. The core mechanism involves systematically exploring the space of possible model geometries using quantum annealing, while simultaneously incorporating a reinforcement learning component to guide the optimization process. We provide a detailed analysis of the proposed method, discussing its theoretical foundations and experimental validation. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications for future research and potential applications.

title: Cognitive Graph Distillation
abstract: This paper introduces Cognitive Graph Distillation, a novel approach for extracting high-level cognitive representations from complex neural networks. The core idea is that the intricate dynamics within large neural networks can be effectively summarized by identifying and prioritizing key nodes and connections, resulting in a simplified graph representation. This distillation process leverages network influence analysis to create a graph that accurately reflects the core cognitive function. Unlike traditional methods focused on feature extraction or weight pruning, Cognitive Graph Distillation offers a fundamentally different perspective, focusing on the relational structure of the network itself. The method's potential lies in providing a means to interpret the internal workings of complex neural networks, potentially leading to new insights into the mechanisms of cognition. We detail the algorithm, its key components, and discuss its potential applications.

title: Cognitive Computing with Semantic Web Technologies and Bayesian Networks
abstract: Current cognitive computing systems often struggle with genuine understanding, relying heavily on pattern recognition and statistical correlations rather than robust semantic comprehension. This paper proposes a novel approach to cognitive computing that addresses this limitation by integrating the strengths of semantic web technologies, specifically Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Web Ontology Language (OWL), with Bayesian Networks. The core idea is to leverage the formal representation of knowledge provided by the semantic web alongside the probabilistic reasoning capabilities of Bayesian Networks. This combined framework allows the system to not only identify patterns but also to reason about complex concepts and relationships, incorporating prior knowledge and explicitly accounting for uncertainty. The architecture presented here offers a significant step towards creating cognitive systems that more closely resemble human thought processes, capable of contextual understanding and adaptive reasoning. We outline the key components of the system and discuss the potential benefits of this integrated approach.

title: Adaptive Metric Learning for Statistical Space
abstract: Develop a method for learning adaptive metrics (distance functions) for statistical space, enabling the efficient representation and analysis of complex, evolving data distributions. This paper presents a novel approach to adaptive metric learning, termed "Dynamic Metric Learning," which dynamically adjusts the metric based on observed data, quantifying the data distribution's shape. We introduce a mechanism to iteratively refine the metric, ensuring a robust representation of the underlying data patterns. This approach is designed to address the challenges of efficiently handling complex, evolving data distributions, offering a new tool for statistical analysis. The paper details the implementation of the Dynamic Metric Learning algorithm, including the key components of the shape quantification mechanism and the optimization strategies employed. The results demonstrate the method's ability to effectively represent and analyze complex data distributions, surpassing the limitations of traditional metric learning techniques.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement Gradient Field (QEFG) - Quantifying Entanglement Evolution
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, exhibits a remarkable degree of correlation between particles, defying classical intuition. However, its practical implications, particularly regarding macroscopic systems, remain largely unexplored. This research investigates the Quantum Entanglement Gradient Field (QEFG) – a novel framework for quantifying the evolution of entanglement through a gradient field, leveraging both quantum mechanics and statistical thermodynamics. The QEFG offers a new lens for understanding the impact of quantum correlations on macroscopic systems, moving beyond simple entanglement measurements. This paper presents a mathematically rigorous model for modeling entanglement as a gradient, incorporating both quantum mechanical principles and statistical thermodynamics to predict entanglement decay and stability. The core mechanism aims to provide a quantitative tool for analyzing entanglement dynamics, opening avenues for potentially significant advancements in our comprehension of quantum phenomena.

title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Information Encoding (DTQE)
abstract: The development of efficient quantum information encoding methods is a crucial area of research in quantum information theory. Traditional approaches often rely on static quantum states, limiting their potential for enhanced storage and transmission efficiency. This paper introduces Dynamic Topology Quantum Information Encoding (DTQE), a novel approach that leverages the topological properties of quantum states to encode information. We propose a method where the inherent topology of a quantum state is dynamically encoded, providing a fundamentally different approach to quantum information processing. This novel technique demonstrates improved storage efficiency and enhanced transmission rates compared to existing encoding schemes. The core of this work lies in the use of topological transformations to map quantum states into a more structured and robust representation, ultimately leading to improved information fidelity and scalability.

title: Dynamic Quantum Control via Feedback Learning Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic quantum control utilizing feedback learning algorithms. The core idea is to develop a system capable of real-time adjustment of control parameters based on feedback information obtained from the quantum system itself. This approach addresses the inherent challenges in precisely controlling quantum systems, which are often highly sensitive to environmental noise and difficult to model accurately. The proposed framework leverages the principles of quantum control and feedback learning to achieve optimal control performance. The system architecture incorporates a closed-loop control mechanism where the system's output is continuously monitored, and the control parameters are adjusted accordingly. Mathematical formulations detailing the control process, feedback mechanisms, and optimization strategies are provided. This work contributes to advancements in quantum control by offering a robust and adaptable method for manipulating quantum states, with potential applications in quantum computing, quantum sensing, and quantum communication. The algorithm is designed to minimize the influence of external disturbances and maximize the accuracy of state preparation and manipulation. The presented approach provides a pathway towards more reliable and efficient quantum control strategies.

title: Graph neural networks and the energetic cavity method for combinatorial optimization
abstract: We study the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) for finding approximate ground states of Ising models. Efficiently finding these ground states is of broad significance because many combinatorial optimization problems can be formulated as an Ising model with the appropriate choice of couplings and fields. Exactly solving these problems is hard but there are many good heuristic methods. A lineage of these heuristics build from mean-field approximations: one approach uses the leading eigenvector of an appropriately defined matrix, another is the min-sum algorithm, also known as the energetic cavity method. Without modification, GNNs perform worse than both of these methods. We consider small modifications to the GNN to incorporate these heuristics and find that this considerably improves performance. While the modified approach is competitive against other deep-learning approaches, we still find that simulated annealing is reliably at least as good as deep learning methods for the same computational cost.

title: CIPHER: Benchmarking Cross-record Inference over Privacy-Hardened Evidence Records
abstract: Reasoning over privacy-constrained records requires combining structured attributes with evidence from free-text narratives. We introduce CIPHER (Cross-record Inference over Privacy-Hardened Evidence Records), a benchmark of expert-validated questions from consumer-finance, clinical, and law-enforcement records. The questions cover common tabular operations and include executable SQL supervision. We evaluate retrieval, prompting, table-specialist, and hybrid symbolic-neural systems under native redaction and surrogate-based evidence restoration. All system families exhibit substantial failures even when supporting records are provided. Most errors arise from incorrect record selection and predicate interpretation rather than arithmetic execution. Privacy transformations have non-uniform effects, sometimes obscuring necessary evidence and sometimes reducing distraction. CIPHER provides a reproducible testbed for diagnosing these failures and assessing how transformations of sensitive text affect reasoning over hybrid records.

title: The Measurement Gap
abstract: This essay argues that the AI capability question posed by "Situational Awareness" (Aschenbrenner, 2024) has, on its own terms, mostly been answered, and has turned into a measurement question that no current benchmark can settle. In the first week of September 2026, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra scored 62.7% and 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark with the same underlying weights, depending only on which evaluation harness was used. This essay treats that result as the central data point. Part I re-grades the 2024 "Situational Awareness" predictions against September 2026 evidence. Part II decomposes the Astra result, defines a "harness ratio" (H) for separating model capability from scaffold-provided capability, and fits a half-life to the ARC-AGI benchmark series (roughly 61 months, 12 months, then 6 months across three generations). Part III proposes DRIFT (Dynamic Rule Inference and Fast Transfer), a benchmark that measures adaptation to unannounced mid-episode rule changes as a rate against a human baseline, rather than a static pass/fail score. A minimum-viable prototype design is included. Part IV states nine dated, falsifiable predictions through September 2028. Written with Claude Fable 5.1 as a research and drafting collaborator; the argument, editing, and any errors are the author's own. All figures were checked against primary sources as of September 7, 2026. Companion site with rendered mathematics: https://measurementgap.com

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithms for Large-Scale Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum-inspired algorithms for tackling large-scale optimization problems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the computational complexity of problems involving numerous variables and constraints. Quantum mechanics, particularly concepts like superposition and entanglement, offers a radically different approach to problem-solving. This work investigates how these concepts can be translated into algorithmic designs, aiming to improve the efficiency and speed of optimization processes. We propose a framework for developing algorithms that mimic quantum phenomena, focusing on techniques that enable exploration of the solution space in a more parallel and potentially faster manner. The core of this approach lies in leveraging mathematical structures derived from quantum mechanics to guide search strategies. We outline key algorithmic ideas, emphasizing the potential for improved convergence rates and scalability. The presented concepts represent a novel application of quantum-inspired ideas to the field of optimization, offering a promising avenue for addressing complex real-world problems.

title: Quantum Probability Field Theory: Adaptive Parameterization
abstract: Quantum probability field theory (QPF) offers a fundamentally different approach to quantum computing and information processing compared to traditional quantum algorithms. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, the adaptive parameterization of quantum probability fields, leveraging quantum entanglement and measurement to dynamically adjust quantum states. We argue that this approach represents a significant step toward achieving more precise quantum state descriptions and calculations, potentially overcoming limitations imposed by current computational paradigms. The core mechanism involves designing a parameterization that responds to quantum measurements, effectively fine-tuning the quantum state through a process of continuous adjustment. This dynamic adjustment aims to enhance the accuracy and robustness of quantum computations, representing a new direction in quantum information theory.

title: Causal Bayesian Networks with Temporal Dynamics
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to representing causal relationships using Causal Bayesian Networks with Temporal Dynamics. Traditional Bayesian Networks, while effective in depicting static causal dependencies, often fail to capture the intricate dynamics of systems influenced by time, feedback loops, and evolving causal links. This work proposes an extension to Bayesian networks that incorporates temporal modeling, allowing for the simulation of system behavior under various interventions and the prediction of future states. The core claim is that representing causal relationships with temporal dynamics significantly enhances the modeling capabilities of Bayesian networks. The key mechanism involves extending the network structure to account for changes in causal dependencies over time. This approach addresses the limitations of static Bayesian networks and provides a more realistic and accurate representation of complex, dynamic systems. The resulting models are capable of predicting system behavior under different interventions, offering significant advantages in fields such as epidemiology, economics, and engineering. The presented framework is designed for flexibility and scalability, accommodating varying degrees of temporal complexity. The paper outlines the core concepts, provides a formal representation of the model, and discusses potential applications.

abstract: This paper investigates the utilization of quantum entanglement to control and optimize topological networks, leveraging the unique properties of entanglement for enhanced network manipulation. Traditional approaches to topological network control often rely on classical computational methods, which are limited by computational complexity. Quantum entanglement offers a potentially transformative mechanism for achieving significantly more efficient and precise control over these complex networks. The core of this work lies in the design and implementation of a control protocol based on manipulating entanglement to induce desired topological transformations. The resulting network's properties are rigorously analyzed and validated, demonstrating the potential of this approach to advance topological network design and control. This research explores the implications of entanglement for network optimization through a novel control mechanism.

title: Information-Theoretic Regularization of Neural Networks
abstract: Deep neural networks, despite their impressive performance, often suffer from an inherent information bottleneck. Standard regularization techniques, such as L1/L2 regularization and dropout, primarily address overfitting by reducing the model's complexity, but they fail to directly tackle the fundamental issue of information loss during the compression of high-dimensional input into lower-dimensional representations. This paper proposes a novel regularization framework that directly addresses this problem by incorporating information-theoretic measures – specifically mutual information and entropy – into the training process. The core idea is to minimize the loss of information during the encoding of the input into the network's internal representations. We introduce a differentiable information-theoretic loss function that can be directly integrated into the network's objective function. This approach provides a principled way to control information flow and, consequently, improve the generalization ability of neural networks. We demonstrate, conceptually, the potential of this method and outline a pathway for future research.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Pareto Dominance-Based Exploration
abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) presents significant challenges due to the difficulty in balancing multiple, often conflicting, objectives. Traditional exploration methods often fail to adequately explore the complex multi-objective action space, leading to suboptimal solutions. This paper proposes a novel exploration strategy for MORL that leverages Pareto dominance to efficiently navigate this space. The core idea is to guide the agent's exploration towards regions where it can achieve better trade-offs between objectives, as defined by Pareto dominance. We formulate the exploration process using a dominance-based ranking of solutions, allowing the agent to systematically identify and target superior solutions. This approach aims to mitigate the "curse of dimensionality" inherent in MORL and improve the convergence towards optimal multi-objective policies. The theoretical framework outlines the key concepts and provides a basis for further research in this area.

title: Causal Machine Learning: A Physics-Based Approach
abstract: Traditional machine learning models often struggle with issues of bias, poor generalization, and a lack of interpretability. These limitations stem from their reliance on purely correlational relationships between variables, without explicitly accounting for underlying causal mechanisms. This paper proposes a novel approach to machine learning – Causal Machine Learning (CML) – that leverages the principles of physics-based causal inference. The core idea is to build machine learning models rooted in causal graphs, enabling the identification and utilization of true causal relationships between variables. This framework allows for more robust model training, improved generalization performance, and enhanced interpretability. We introduce a methodology for constructing causal models from observational data, focusing on techniques for identifying and quantifying causal effects. The resulting models are then used for prediction and, crucially, for understanding the underlying mechanisms driving the observed data. This approach addresses key challenges in traditional machine learning by incorporating a fundamentally more realistic representation of the world – one governed by causal laws. We demonstrate the potential benefits of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline future research directions.

title: Fractal-Based Representation of Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to analyzing and designing neural network architectures by leveraging the principles of fractal geometry. The core idea is to represent the intricate connections and layered structure of a neural network as a fractal. This representation allows for a more intuitive understanding of architectural complexity, facilitates the identification of critical bottlenecks, and potentially guides the design of more efficient and robust networks. We outline a mapping methodology and explore the potential benefits of this fractal-based approach, focusing on the inherent self-similarity properties of fractals. The resulting fractal structure provides a powerful tool for visualizing and quantifying network architecture, offering a new perspective on optimization and design. Further research will explore the application of fractal analysis to various neural network designs and its impact on performance metrics.

title: Self-Organizing Constraint System for Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-organizing constraint system for evolutionary algorithms designed to enhance solution fitness through dynamic constraint adjustment. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often rely on predefined constraints, which can limit the search space and hinder optimization. Our approach dynamically modifies constraints based on the algorithm's progress, allowing the system to intelligently guide the search towards more promising solutions. We detail the core mechanism, including a fitness monitoring loop and constraint modification strategy. The benefits of this system, including improved convergence speed and solution quality, are explored, with a focused discussion on its practical implications. Keywords: Evolutionary Algorithms, Constraint System, Dynamic Adjustment, Fitness Optimization, Self-Organization.

title: Neural Symbolic Hybrid Systems for Robust Reasoning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence by integrating neural networks and symbolic reasoning, resulting in Neural Symbolic Hybrid Systems. The core claim is that combining the strengths of both paradigms—the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks and the logical inference capabilities of symbolic systems—yields more robust and explainable AI systems. The proposed system utilizes neural networks for perceptual tasks, such as feature extraction and initial data interpretation, while employing symbolic reasoning engines for higher-level logical inference, decision-making, and knowledge representation. The system architecture is designed to facilitate seamless interaction between these two components. Specifically, the neural network outputs are translated into symbolic representations, which are then processed by the reasoning engine. Conversely, the symbolic reasoning engine's conclusions are fed back into the neural network for refinement and improved accuracy. This hybrid approach addresses limitations inherent in purely neural or purely symbolic systems. Neural networks alone can lack explainability and robustness against noisy or incomplete data, while symbolic systems often struggle with complex, real-world scenarios requiring flexible pattern recognition. This paper outlines the core mechanisms, architecture, and potential benefits of such a system, highlighting its capacity for robust reasoning and enhanced interpretability. The system is envisioned as a significant step towards developing more reliable and trustworthy AI solutions.

title: Dynamic Programming for Quantum Circuit Optimization with Uncertainty
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a crucial step in realizing the full potential of quantum computing. However, the inherent uncertainty in quantum gate fidelities and measurement outcomes presents a significant challenge. Traditional optimization methods often fail to adequately address this probabilistic nature. This paper proposes a novel dynamic programming approach for quantum circuit optimization that explicitly incorporates uncertainty. The algorithm constructs an optimal circuit path by minimizing the expected cost, which accounts for the potential error associated with each gate operation and measurement. This framework allows for a more accurate and robust optimization process, leading to circuits with reduced error and improved performance. The core claim is that dynamic programming can be effectively applied to quantum circuit optimization, acknowledging and utilizing the probabilistic elements. The key mechanism involves a structured, iterative process to evaluate and select the best circuit paths based on a quantified uncertainty model. This approach avoids the limitations of purely deterministic optimization techniques when dealing with quantum systems.

title: Lost in Explanation: Can Cognitive Forcing Counteract Over-Reliance Across Sentiment, Irony, and Sarcasm?
abstract: While explanations in AI-assisted decision-making are intended to build trust, they can also cause users to over-rely on incorrect predictions. We investigate whether this effect changes depending on how subjective the underlying NLP task is. We present participants with sentences varying in subjectivity—sentiment, irony, and sarcasm—and ask them to judge the intended meaning. Each participant completes all three explanation conditions—no explanation (Control), a standard explanation (Standard NLE), or an explanation that also points to a plausible alternative reading (Cognitive Forcing NLE)—with condition order counterbalanced across participants. Participants first give an initial judgment, then see the model's prediction accompanied by the explanation for that condition (if any), and finally give a final decision. We test whether over-reliance increases with task subjectivity (H1), whether a standard explanation increases over-reliance relative to no explanation (H2), whether an explanation surfacing an alternative reading reduces over-reliance relative to a standard explanation (H3), and, exploratively, whether this reduction is larger for more subjective tasks (H4). This study is conducted as part of the Natural Language Processing 2 course at the University of Regensburg.

title: <!--Does This Affect the Interpretation of What Follows?-->
abstract: By defining the content of formal ontologies, we can determine, for the ontology, the truth value of any statement that refers to, or does not refer to, that content. This is not possible for all XML documents. The main reason for this is that, unlike ontologies, XML does not inherently embrace any principle for handling known and unknown information as a metalanguage. This allows the application of different principles to the same XML document, which generate different interpretations of it, thereby undermining the communication between people and software applications that XML, like ontologies, is supposed to support. In this paper, I propose a solution for XML documents to come close to achieving the same result as ontologies: including comments that contain principles for handling known and unknown information. In demonstrating that this solution works only under very specific circumstances, I also focus on the communication that ontologies and XML documents are intended to support, highlighting the different roles they assign to the subjects engaging with their content: spectators and interpreters, respectively. More specifically, I argue that the fact that the subjects (whether people or software applications) have ultimate authority over the interpretation of XML documents renders the documents hermeneutically unstable – an instability that even the inclusion of a comment specifying a principle for handling known and unknown information shifts rather than definitively resolves.

title: Dimensionality Reduction Networks and Autoencoders
abstract: Autoencoders (AEs) have become indispensable tools for a wide range of DIP tasks, including feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and noise filtering. This chapter provides a comprehensive introduction to various linear and nonlinear AEs. We begin by presenting a linear AE network that implements Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using a modified Hebbian learning rule, alongside an efficient recursive least squares (RLS)-based unsupervised learning approach for sequential PCA extraction. As for nonlinear approaches, we introduce two separate lines of approaches, including a manifold learning method based on Laplacian Eigenmaps with incremental novel sample embedding capability. We then explore a wide variety of deterministic and stochastic nonlinear AEs, such as basic, sparse, denoising, and contrastive. Furthermore, the relationship between AEs and manifold learning is discussed. Finally, numerous practical examples are included to highlight the real-life applicability of these networks. The chapter concludes with several computer projects and challenging problems.

title: MoM: Memory of Memory
abstract: For a long-horizon LLM agent, the memory question is not what was once recorded but what currently holds. Most designs answer it only indirectly: every interaction is stored, and the present is reconstructed at query time by retrieving and reconciling records, so stale values re-enter and the same conflicts are re-litigated. Committing the current value at write time avoids this, but existing write-time (CRUD) memories overwrite, so a wrong update is unrecoverable and prior state is lost. We take the missing combination---commit on arrival while retaining what is displaced---and formalize it as Memory of Memory (MoM): memory tracks not only content but the provenance, status, and history of its own entries. We instantiate MoM as Provenant Memory (P-Mem), a typed provenance graph whose active frontier exposes one current value per resolved key while displaced values are retained as provenance; typed operations decide whether a new observation supports, supersedes, contests, rejects, revokes, or resolves an existing value. P-Mem's decisive gain is validity rather than accuracy: its turn-level read matches the strongest retrieval memory in accuracy at sim4times fewer read tokens---a retrieval-granularity effect---while graph-guided turn pruning cuts the knowledge-update stale-answer rate (19.4\%rightarrow10.9\%); on revision chains it stays at 100\% where query-time reading collapses to 25\%, and, because displaced values are retained rather than overwritten, it recovers committed errors a CRUD memory cannot (100\% vs.\ 0\%).

title: Propaq: A Python package for Heisenberg Propagation
abstract: We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.

title: Conditioned Initialization for Attention
abstract: Transformers are a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, powering applications across vision, language, and beyond. At the core of their success lies the attention layer, where the query, key, and value matrices determine how token dependencies are captured. While considerable work has focused on scaling and optimizing Transformers, comparatively little attention has been paid to how the weights of the queries, keys and values are initialized. Common practice relies on random initialization or alternatives such as mimetic initialization, which imitates weight patterns from converged models, and weight selection, which transfers weights from a teacher model. In this paper, we argue that initialization can introduce an optimization bias that fundamentally shapes training dynamics. We propose conditioned initialization, a principled scheme that initializes attention weights to improve the spectral properties of the attention layer. evidence.abstract: Transformers are a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, powering applications across vision, language, and beyond. At the core of their success lies the attention layer, where the query, key, and value matrices determine how token dependencies are captured. title: Federated Neuro-Symbolic Learning for Privacy-Preserving Intelligent Edge Systems
abstract: Intelligent Edge Systems – smart cameras, wearable technology, connected cars and industrial sensors – are creating a growing need to learn from local data at the edge. The two main lines of research that have attempted to address this problem differ. On one hand, Federated Learning (FL) enables training of common models based on the raw data remaining on each device. FL protects user privacy since the model parameters never leave the device. However, FL produces "opaque" (statistical-only) predictors that fail to generalize well in the presence of data heterogeneity and that provide no formal guarantees. On the other hand, Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) learning combines neural perception (e.g., deep neural networks for image classification) with symbolic reasoning, resulting in models that are both efficient with regard to data usage and interpretable, and that are capable of encoding a priori domain knowledge (rules). While NeSy learning has been primarily studied within centralized environments and therefore does not take into consideration the challenges associated with distributed or decentralized learning (such as edge-based intelligent systems), we propose a new paradigm called Federated Neuro-Symbolic Learning (FNSL) for the purpose of enabling NeSy models to be learned in a Federated environment while maintaining formal privacy protection. In our proposed framework, each client (a representative edge system) contains a neural encoder which feeds the encoded information into a differentiable symbolic reasoner. Our server collects masked neural parameter updates from clients and uses this information to refine a collective symbolic knowledge base. To protect users' data and maintain differential privacy during the process of collecting parameter updates, we use secure aggregation methods. Moreover, we adaptively weight domain knowledge according to the confidence assigned to each symbolically represented rule. We demonstrate through experiments using image, sensor and tabular benchmark datasets and non-IID partitioning schemes that FNSL achieves improvements of 4-7 percentage points in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art FL baselines. Additionally, we show that FNSL reduces the amount of uplink communication required per iteration by more than 50%. Lastly, we examine how tightly enforcing privacy budgets impacts performance.

title: Quantum Entanglement Orchestration: A Novel Algorithmic Approach to Self-Organization
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a peculiar phenomenon where two or more particles become linked, presents a paradigm shift in our understanding of information and computation. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to design a novel algorithmic approach to self-organization, specifically focusing on optimizing and controlling complex systems. Our core claim posits the design of a quantum self-organization algorithm predicated on the unique properties of entanglement. We delve into the mechanism of this algorithm, emphasizing the utilization of quantum superposition and entanglement for optimization and control, demonstrating its potential to surpass the capabilities of existing classical self-organization techniques.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Programming for Complex Optimization
abstract: Quantum-enhanced constraint programming (QCP) presents a novel approach to tackling complex optimization problems by integrating quantum algorithms into the constraint programming framework. This paper explores the potential of quantum annealing and quantum approximate optimization algorithms (QAOA) to accelerate solution exploration and enhance the ability to find optimal solutions for challenging problems. We detail the core mechanism, highlighting its advantages over classical methods in navigating high-dimensional constraint spaces and potential for improved performance in diverse optimization scenarios. The study focuses on demonstrating the efficacy of this technique through illustrative examples, showcasing the benefits of leveraging quantum resources for complex optimization.

title: Self-Adaptive Graph Theory Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive graph theory optimization algorithm designed to enhance model generalization. Traditional graph structure optimization methods often rely on static approaches, while this algorithm dynamically adjusts graph structure based on node and edge characteristics, leading to more robust and adaptable models. We propose a method that iteratively refines the graph topology, incorporating feedback from model performance to mitigate overfitting and promote better generalization. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of graph structures to automatically optimize the model's representation, resulting in improved performance across diverse datasets. This research focuses on providing a practical and effective solution for complex model optimization tasks.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive graph theory framework for distributed probability inference, designed to enhance reasoning efficiency and accuracy through dynamic graph structure learning. title: Adaptive Representation Learning for Streaming Data with Memory Constraints
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive representation learning framework tailored for streaming data environments constrained by limited memory. The core challenge in applying traditional representation learning techniques to continuous data streams lies in the need to retain sufficient information while managing computational resources. Our approach addresses this issue through a dynamically pruning and growing representation, effectively balancing accuracy and efficiency. We introduce a mechanism where a minimal core representation is maintained, and new features are selectively added based on their impact on performance or the evolving data distribution. This adaptive strategy allows the model to continually refine its representation without incurring excessive memory overhead. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, providing a robust solution for representation learning in resource-scarce streaming data scenarios. The key innovations include the dynamic pruning and growing strategy, the feature selection criterion based on performance improvement and distribution adaptation, and the overall architecture designed for efficient memory usage. This work contributes to the field by offering a practical and scalable approach to representation learning for streaming data, addressing a critical limitation in existing methods.

title: 拓扑结构驱动的机器学习模型
abstract: This paper introduces a novel machine learning model leveraging topological structure to dynamically adjust parameters and enhance model generalization. Traditional machine learning often relies on fixed parameter settings, limiting the model's ability to adapt to diverse data. We propose a method where the model's internal structure, represented as a topological graph, guides the optimization process. This approach enables the model to automatically fine-tune its parameters based on the specific characteristics of the input data, resulting in improved performance across a broader range of datasets. The core mechanism involves constructing a topological graph representing the data distribution and using this graph to guide the optimization of model parameters. This allows the model to identify and exploit underlying patterns within the data, leading to more robust and adaptable learning. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both accuracy and generalization. We believe this approach offers a significant advancement in machine learning, particularly for tasks requiring adaptability and robust performance.

title: Fractal Neural Networks for Hierarchical Feature Extraction
abstract: This paper introduces Fractal Neural Networks (FNNs) as a novel approach to hierarchical feature extraction within deep learning. Traditional neural network architectures, while effective, often struggle to efficiently capture complex, multi-scale hierarchical relationships within data. FNNs address this limitation by employing a fractal-inspired design, utilizing recursive, self-similar layers to create nested representations of the input. The core claim is that this structural approach enables more efficient and effective hierarchical feature learning. The proposed architecture mirrors the branching patterns found in fractals, where each layer operates on a downsampled version of the input, generating increasingly abstract and refined representations. We detail the mathematical formulation and key concepts underpinning FNNs, demonstrating their potential to outperform conventional networks in tasks requiring the extraction of intricate hierarchical features. The presented framework offers a fundamentally different perspective on hierarchical learning, promising improved performance and potentially reducing computational complexity.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Cooperative Reward Shaping
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) presents significant challenges due to the difficulty in designing reward functions that effectively encourage collaboration. Traditional reward structures frequently lead to inefficient learning, as agents may prioritize individual gains over collective success. This paper proposes a novel approach to address this issue: dynamic reward shaping. Our method dynamically adjusts the reward function based on the overall progress of the multi-agent system, providing more immediate and relevant feedback to agents. This mechanism fosters better coordination and ultimately leads to more efficient learning and improved performance in cooperative tasks. We detail the theoretical underpinnings, the algorithm design, and discuss potential applications. The key contributions include a formally defined dynamic reward shaping framework and a corresponding algorithm for its implementation. We demonstrate, through a theoretical analysis and simplified examples, the efficacy of this approach compared to static reward shaping.

title: Deep Learning-Based Program Formal Verification (DLBFV)
abstract: This paper proposes Deep Learning-Based Program Formal Verification (DLBFV), a novel approach leveraging the power of deep learning to enhance the efficiency and coverage of program formal verification. Traditional program verification techniques often struggle with the complexity and scale of modern software, leading to limitations in both speed and thoroughness. DLBFV addresses this challenge by training a deep learning model to learn semantic information from program code and subsequently utilize this knowledge for automated formal verification. title: Probabilistic Relational Programming with Bayesian Graph Embeddings
abstract: This paper introduces a novel programming paradigm, Probabilistic Relational Programming with Bayesian Graph Embeddings (PRP-GBE), designed to address the challenges of representing and reasoning with complex relational knowledge. The core problem lies in the "curse of dimensionality" inherent in traditional probabilistic models when dealing with intricate relational structures. Our approach combines Relational Programming, which provides a natural way to express relationships between entities, with Bayesian Graph Embeddings, which learn compact, low-dimensional representations of these graphs. Nodes in the graph represent entities and are associated with continuous probability distributions, while edges represent relations also parameterized by these distributions. The Bayesian graph embeddings effectively learn a latent space that significantly reduces the computational complexity of probabilistic inference and learning tasks. This integration allows for direct probabilistic reasoning within relational data structures, offering a potentially powerful solution for knowledge representation, reasoning, and ultimately, more robust and adaptable AI systems. We present a foundational framework for PRP-GBE, detailing the core components and outlining potential applications.

title: Adaptive Optimization of Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Quantum algorithms, renowned for their potential to solve complex problems beyond the capabilities of classical computers, often exhibit inherent sensitivity to initial conditions and parameter choices. We introduce a framework that leverages quantum algorithm properties to automatically refine parameter settings, thereby maximizing efficiency and exploring a broader range of solution spaces. This approach aims to surpass the limitations of traditional optimization techniques by proactively addressing the unique challenges posed by quantum computation.

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to matrix optimization utilizing a dynamically adjusted topology. We propose a self-adaptive learning algorithm that leverages the inherent non-linear properties of matrix operations to optimize complex matrices. The core mechanism centers around constructing a dynamic topology that responds to the matrix's state, allowing the system to adjust its behavior in real-time. This approach offers a promising path towards intelligent system design, addressing limitations of traditional optimization methods. The paper details the algorithm's design, its mathematical framework, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a simplified, yet illustrative, scenario.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Algorithm Design and Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the design and optimization of algorithms within the burgeoning field of quantum machine learning (QML). The core aim is to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of QML techniques by proposing novel algorithmic approaches and implementing effective optimization strategies. We investigate various methods, including quantum support vector machines (QSVMs), quantum principal component analysis (QPCA), and quantum neural networks (QNNs), focusing on how to leverage quantum properties such as superposition and entanglement to accelerate learning processes and potentially surpass the limitations of classical algorithms. The optimization strategies discussed encompass both algorithmic refinements and the selection of appropriate quantum hardware architectures. The results presented demonstrate the potential of tailored QML algorithms to achieve significant improvements in specific machine learning tasks. Further research is needed to fully realize the transformative capabilities of QML, but this work provides a foundational understanding and a roadmap for future development.

title: Spectral Criterion for Disorder-Free Localization of Quantum Walks on Hypercube: QBN Approach
abstract: We study disorder-free localization in a spin-coupled quantum walk on the hypercube within the quantum Bernoulli noises framework. We derive a general criterion for disorder-free localization: it occurs if and only if some spectral subspace of a reduced unitary evolution contains a vector whose position marginal probability is non-uniform. For the Grover walk with distance-dependent coupling \(ϕ_σ=|σ|π/(n+1)\) in dimension \(d=4\), we explicitly construct a non-uniform fixed point in the all \(+1\) spin configuration. This implies that disorder-free localization occurs in our model.

title: Exponentiated gradients support effective learning in biologically relevant scenarios
abstract: Keynote address. Computational neuroscience relies on gradient descent (GD) for training artificial neural network (ANN) models of the brain. The advantage of GD is that it is effective at learning difficult tasks. However, it produces ANNs that are a poor phenomenological fit to biology, making them less relevant as models of the brain. Specifically, it violates Dale's law, by allowing synapses to change from excitatory to inhibitory, and leads to synaptic weights that are not log-normally distributed, contradicting experimental data. Here, starting from first principles of optimization theory, I will present an alternative learning algorithm, exponentiated gradient (EG), that respects Dale's Law and produces log-normal weights, without losing the power of learning with gradients. We show that in biologically relevant settings EG outperforms GD, including learning from sparsely relevant signals and dealing with synaptic pruning. Altogether, our results show that EG is a superior learning algorithm for modelling the brain with ANNs.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Internal Feedback Loops
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to training neural networks – Self-Correcting Neural Networks (SCNNs) – designed to mitigate the challenges of drifting gradients and inaccurate representations often encountered during extended training. The core concept involves integrating internal feedback loops within the network architecture. These loops continuously monitor the output of specific layers and, leveraging a learned error signal, dynamically adjust the weights to correct deviations from desired behavior. This creates a self-correcting mechanism, fostering greater stability and robustness. The theoretical framework details the mathematical formulation of the correction process, highlighting the role of the error signal and the iterative weight adjustment. The proposed SCNN architecture offers a promising pathway towards more reliable and efficient neural network training, particularly for complex tasks and long training durations. The key contribution lies in providing a demonstrable method for inherent self-correction, addressing a significant limitation of traditional neural network training methodologies. ---

title: 基于量子密钥分发协议的密码学体系
abstract: This paper introduces a novel cryptographic system based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) principles. Traditional cryptographic methods are vulnerable to attacks from both classical and quantum computers. This research explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement and key distribution to establish a fundamentally secure communication channel. We propose a QKD-based system leveraging quantum entanglement for secure key exchange and decryption, analyzing its security properties and potential advantages over existing cryptographic techniques. The core claim focuses on the enhanced security afforded by quantum mechanics, specifically the vulnerability of classical encryption to attacks leveraging the inherent properties of entangled states. The paper details the design of the QKD protocol, its security analysis, and potential applications within a secure communication framework.

abstract: This paper explores the application of adaptive machine learning to incorporate domain knowledge into model representations. Traditional machine learning models often struggle to effectively leverage domain knowledge, limiting their performance and interpretability. This work proposes a novel framework that dynamically embeds domain knowledge into the model during training, improving generalization and providing enhanced explainability. We detail the core mechanisms behind this approach, including a modular architecture and iterative refinement strategies, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of simulated and experimental studies. The core claim is that this framework significantly enhances model performance and interpretability, addressing the limitations of traditional approaches.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning for Robotics
abstract: Quantum-enhanced reinforcement learning (QEL) offers the potential to significantly improve the performance of robotic systems, particularly in navigating complex environments and adapting to dynamic situations. This paper explores the integration of quantum computing with reinforcement learning to accelerate learning, enhance exploration, and improve adaptation. We propose a novel approach that leverages quantum annealing and quantum reinforcement learning to overcome the limitations of classical RL in challenging scenarios. The core claim is that combining these two paradigms will lead to enhanced robot navigation and control capabilities. The study focuses on demonstrating the effectiveness of this combined approach through simulations and preliminary results.
